SyclKittens: A Tile Programming Model for Programmers and Coding Agents on Intel GPUs

CCS: Computing methodologies Parallel programming languagesCCS: Computer systems organization Single instruction, multiple data
Yehong Jiang email: yehong28@mit.edu Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA Note: Work performed while the author was an intern at Intel Corporation. , Sheng Chen email: sheng.s.chen@intel.com Affiliation: Intel Corporation, Shanghai, China , Fangwen Fu email: fangwen.fu@intel.com Affiliation: Intel Corporation, Santa Clara, California, USA , Yen-Kuang Chen email: y.k.chen@intel.com Affiliation: Intel Corporation, Santa Clara, California, USA , Xinmin Tian email: xinmin.tian@intel.com Affiliation: Intel Corporation, Santa Clara, California, USA , Stuart H. Sul email: ssul@stanford.edu Affiliation: Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA and Simran Arora email: simarora@caltech.edu Affiliation: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California, USA
Abstract.

New AI accelerators arrive before the kernels that make them fast, because peak kernel performance requires architecture-specific expertise in operand pipelines and data-movement techniques. Coding agents can now write, compile, and tune kernels on their own, so they could greatly accelerate kernel development and optimization. What agents produce depends on the interfaces they are given. These interfaces may expose a machine’s raw capabilities or encode the known-good methods for exploiting its hardware features efficiently. We test the performance impact of these two interfaces on Intel GPUs through controlled experiments with three coding models on three kernels. With raw SYCL and execution feedback, Opus 4.8, the strongest of the three models tested, writes a single-GPU GEMM kernel reaching only 57.5%57.5\% of Intel’s tuned oneDNN library. We present SyclKittens, a hardware-aware tile programming model for Intel GPUs that encodes these known-good methods, so its operations place operands in matrix-engine layouts, prefetch through the L1 cache, and communicate over the fabric that links GPU stacks into a node. With SyclKittens under the same agent, task, and feedback budget, the agent reaches 82.1%82.1\%, showing that encoded methods turn hardware capabilities into performance. Workload-specific policies stay programmable, and engineers and agents jointly refine these schedules in SyclKittens to build a kernel suite that reaches ∼96%{\sim}96\% of oneDNN in geometric mean across GEMM shapes. The suite runs Llama-3.1-8B inference 1.59×1.59\times faster than torch.compile on one GPU and up to 2.91×2.91\times faster than a matched multi-GPU decode path on Intel’s oneCCL. SyclKittens is open source and available at https://github.com/intel/SyclKittens.

Keywords: 
SyclKittens, tile-based programming, GPU kernel optimization, performance portability, SYCL, coding agents, Intel Max GPU, LLM inference

1. Introduction

Supporting diverse AI hardware is limited by the difficulty of building high-performance kernel ecosystems. Tile programming models such as ThunderKittens and HipKittens package architecture-specific methods for NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, while ParallelKittens extends this approach for multiple GPUs (Spector et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Sul et al., 2025). Coding agents can improve programs through execution feedback, and kernel benchmarks show that they can write, compile, benchmark, and revise single- and multi-GPU kernels (Yang et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2025; Chan et al., 2026). We ask whether a tile programming model can make Intel GPU methods reusable by programmers and coding agents while preserving workload-specific control.

In our study, three agentic-coding models produce correct Intel GPU kernels that are substantially slower than the tuned baselines. They use raw SYCL, a C++ programming model for heterogeneous systems (Khronos Group, 2026). The tasks are single-GPU matrix multiplication (GEMM), causal grouped-query attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023), and distributed GEMM. Each model receives Intel documentation and execution feedback and works autonomously under a fixed search budget. On single-GPU GEMM, Opus 4.8 produces the fastest raw-SYCL kernel among the three models, but it reaches only 57.5% of the throughput of oneDNN, Intel’s tuned deep-learning library (oneDNN Project, 2024). Its kernel already uses the GPU’s matrix engines and fetches operands ahead of computation. However, its thread groups do not coordinate prefetching and repeatedly request the same operand tiles.

We introduce SyclKittens, a hardware-aware tile programming model for Intel GPUs. We target the Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550 (Intel Max GPU) (Intel Corporation, 2023b; Blythe, 2021), deployed in Aurora (Allcock et al., 2025). The tile interface must match the packed register layouts of Xe Matrix Extensions (XMX), Intel’s matrix engines, and coordinate operand delivery through cache prefetch and 2-D block loads. Communication operations must account for the bandwidth difference between MDFI (Multi-Die Fabric Interconnect), the faster link between the two GPU stacks within a package, and XeLink, the peer load/store network between packages. Built with Intel hardware experts, SyclKittens extends the tile abstractions of ThunderKittens and dataflow algorithms from ThunderKittens and HipKittens with three classes of Intel-specific operations.

  1. (1)

    Matrix operand layouts and packing. SyclKittens maps register tiles to XMX’s native execution width and fuses 2-D block loads with hardware packing for the column-layout right-hand matrix operand B, avoiding software packing shuffles. In the cumulative GEMM ablation, changing from 16×1616\times 16 to 32×3232\times 32 register tiles raises geometric-mean throughput from 37.4%37.4\% to 68.2%68.2\% of oneDNN across 27 shapes (§3).

  2. (2)

    Cooperative cache prefetch. Tile-level prefetch lets groups of threads prefetch disjoint regions of shared operands into the L1 cache while computing. In our tuned GEMM, replacing heuristic prefetch coordination with disjoint ownership raises geometric-mean throughput from 91.0%91.0\% to 96.2%96.2\% of oneDNN (§3).

  3. (3)

    Topology-aware GPU communication. To avoid repeated XeLink transfers, SyclKittens gathers each shard once per remote package and replicates it over MDFI. This yields 1.42–2.15 times the end-to-end distributed-GEMM throughput of the flat gather pipeline (§3).

Raw SYCL exposes hardware capabilities, including matrix instructions, prefetch, and peer memory. SyclKittens encodes methods that coordinate these capabilities. Programmers and coding agents choose workload policies, including tile shape, prefetch ownership and distance, and work distribution (Figure 1(a)). An accelerator interface should encode the architecture’s methods as first-class operations while leaving workload policy programmable.

We perform three evaluations of SyclKittens. Controlled coding-agent experiments test whether encoding Intel-specific methods in the programming model helps agents produce faster kernels. The kernel-suite evaluation tests whether these abstractions support high performance across a broad range of operations. The inference evaluation measures whether those kernels deliver end-to-end gains for Llama-3.1-8B on single and multiple GPUs.

  • •

    For controlled coding-agent experiments, we vary programming context under a fixed feedback protocol. The first context, Raw SYCL (Raw), provides Intel documentation. The second context, SyclKittens, adds its headers and interface documentation. The third context, SyclKittens + examples, provides kernel source code for NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, or for different operations on Intel GPUs. For Opus, the best-performing context on each task is either SyclKittens or SyclKittens + examples. Single-GPU GEMM performance rises from 57.5%57.5\% of oneDNN under Raw to 82.1%82.1\% with SyclKittens. In cold iteration, where agents start from scratch, SyclKittens helps Opus reach Raw’s final performance with fewer tuning steps (Figure 1(b)). For GQA, Opus reaches 79.5%79.5\% of PyTorch’s native scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) with SyclKittens + examples, up from 57.7%57.7\% with Raw SYCL. All selected Opus GQA kernels use XMX across the three contexts. The examples help the agent find more effective execution schedules.

  • •

    We build a high-performance kernel suite with SyclKittens through engineer-agent co-design. The suite reaches ∼96%{\sim}96\% of oneDNN in geometric mean across all 27 GEMM shapes. On causal multi-head attention (MHA) (Vaswani et al., 2017), SyclKittens delivers 1.21×1.21\times the geometric-mean throughput of fused SDPA with Intel Extension for PyTorch (IPEX). The suite also includes normalization, rotary position embedding (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV), multi-GPU collectives, and fused distributed kernels.

  • •

    We evaluate Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori and others, 2024) inference on one GPU and on a full Intel Max node with six two-stack packages (12 GPUs). (i) On one GPU, SyclKittens works alongside torch.compile, improving full-request prefill-plus-decode throughput by 1.59×1.59\times in geometric mean over torch.compile alone. SyclKittens also runs configurations where torch.compile alone runs out of memory. (ii) At node scale, SyclKittens combines tensor-parallel projections (Shoeybi et al., 2019) with context-parallel attention. Its decode implementation outperforms the tuned inference path built on Intel’s oneCCL collective-communication library, by up to 2.91×2.91\times on four GPUs, and serves longer contexts than the baseline can fit in memory (§6).

This paper makes three contributions.

  1. (1)

    We build and open-source SyclKittens, an Intel GPU tile programming model that encodes architectural methods while preserving workload control, and quantify their performance contributions through GEMM ablations (§3).

  2. (2)

    We provide a controlled coding-agent study that isolates the effects of encoded methods, example kernels, and execution feedback on kernel performance and workload-policy search (§4).

  3. (3)

    We present a co-designed Intel GPU kernel suite and evaluate its performance in individual kernels and Llama-3.1-8B inference (§5.2, §6).

2. Background and Motivation

2.1. Tile Programming and Coding Agents

Tile programming models expose fixed-shape register and shared-memory tiles, layouts that address larger tensors in memory, and bulk movement, matrix, reduction, and synchronization operations. They sit between tensor compilers, which choose most schedules, and low-level GPU programming, which exposes individual lanes and instructions. This middle layer separates tile-level algorithms from the architecture-specific layouts, movement, and scheduling that realize them. ThunderKittens (Spector et al., 2025) and HipKittens (Hu et al., 2025) provide hardware-aware interfaces on NVIDIA and AMD, respectively, and their shared primitives provide the conceptual starting point for SyclKittens. A prior IWOCL study ported ThunderKittens directly to SYCL for Intel kernels on a single GPU (Jiang et al., 2026). SyclKittens extends that work with the Intel-specific operations in §3, including partial-tile cooperative prefetch and topology-aware communication, and evaluates their use in full-model inference.

Other systems divide control between the programmer and the compiler differently. CuTe/CUTLASS provides fine-grained layout and thread-participation control through C++ templates (NVIDIA, 2024; NVIDIA, 2025), while TileLang separates tile dataflow from schedule selection (Wang et al., 2025). For Intel GPUs, programmers can use portable SYCL (Khronos Group, 2026), explicit SIMD (ESIMD) vectors (Intel Corporation, 2023a), compiler-selected Triton schedules through Intel’s XPU backend (Tillet et al., 2019; Intel Corporation, 2026), or template libraries with native hardware control, such as XeTLA (Intel Corporation, 2023c) and SYCL-TLA (Intel Corporation, 2025c). Intel’s oneAPI toolchain also provides joint_matrix, a portable SYCL extension that drives matrix engines while hiding the operand layouts SyclKittens makes explicit.

At node scale, ParallelKittens (Sul et al., 2025) extends ThunderKittens to multiple GPUs and composes communication with computation through NVIDIA interconnects. Intel oneCCL provides tuned collective operations (UXL Foundation, 2025). SyclKittens exposes peer-memory operations and synchronization within kernels so that programmers can coordinate data movement with computation across Intel GPU stacks and packages. These operations let kernels overlap communication with attention in the manner of ring attention (Liu et al., 2024).

AI coding agents can generate and iteratively improve programs, but for GPU kernels, correctness and performance are separate objectives. KernelBench (Ouyang et al., 2025) evaluates fast, correct single-GPU kernel generation over 250 PyTorch workloads. ParallelKernelBench (Chan et al., 2026) extends the setting to multi-GPU PyTorch+NCCL baselines and fine-grained CUDA or DSL kernels. Both establish that execution and profiling feedback help. Our controlled study on Intel GPUs separates the effect of the tile interface from that of example kernels. Raw SYCL and SyclKittens test the interface change; SyclKittens and SyclKittens + examples test the additional source examples under the matched protocol in §4.

2.2. Intel GPU Model

We study the Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550 (Intel Max GPU) (Intel Corporation, 2023b; Blythe, 2021; Jiang, 2022; Allcock et al., 2025). Each package is one PCIe device built from two stacks, Intel’s term for its physical GPU tiles. We run the flat device hierarchy, so each stack is exposed as its own SYCL device with 56 Xe cores and 64 GB of HBM2e, and a node presents 12 stacks across 6 packages. In workload and performance descriptions, we call each exposed stack a GPU; we reserve stack and package for the physical topology. Throughout this paper, tile refers only to a register or shared tile in the language, and not to a partition of the hardware. Figure 2 summarizes the stack and node hierarchy, and the three hardware properties discussed below shape the SyclKittens design in §3.

Execution and registers.

Intel software addresses register operands as linear vectors along the SIMD direction, one element per lane, whereas NVIDIA tensor-core interfaces use matrix fragments distributed across a warp. The shared tile abstractions therefore require different physical register layouts on the two architectures. A subgroup is the SIMD execution group within a workgroup. The Intel Max GPU supports 16- or 32-lane subgroups, while its Xe Matrix Extensions (XMX) matrix engines only consume 16-lane subgroups. When all 16 lanes move one four-byte register element, the subgroup access spans exactly one 64-byte cache line. These execution and transaction widths determine the register-tile mapping in §3.2.

Operand delivery.

The Intel Max GPU supports direct matrix-operand delivery through the cache hierarchy. A hardware 2-D prefetch warms an L1 cache of up to 512 KB per Xe core, and a 2-D demand load then moves the cached operand into subgroup registers. Shared local memory (SLM) remains available. The SyclKittens matrix path studied here uses L1 prefetch and 2-D demand loads without intermediate SLM staging (Figure 2(a)). This differs from the asynchronous global-to-shared-memory staging used by ThunderKittens.

Node fabric.

The Multi-Die Fabric Interconnect (MDFI) links the two GPU stacks within a package. XeLink, Intel’s peer load/store network between packages, connects packages all-to-all through independent even- and odd-stack planes. Together, these fabrics allow any pair of stacks to communicate directly (Figure 2(b)). Multicast and reduction are composed in software over these peer paths. XeLink also provides per-link copy engines for explicit transfers. However, peer-to-peer communications over these fabrics differ in bandwidth and the number of transfers they can sustain concurrently. MDFI provides substantially higher bandwidth than XeLink. Same-plane traffic uses a direct XeLink path, while cross-plane traffic traverses an additional MDFI link. In distributed GEMM, a topology-aware gather that crosses XeLink once per remote package and replicates over MDFI delivers 1.421.42–2.15×2.15\times the end-to-end throughput of the flat gather pipeline (§3.4). Appendix A reports measurement methods, full values, and a cross-vendor terminology map.

The tile interface separates algorithmic operations from their architecture-specific lowering. Intel’s upcoming Crescent Island data center GPU illustrates which hardware properties a new lowering must consider. It is based on the Intel Xe3p architecture, which retains matrix engines and an L1 operand path (Mohan and Jiang, 2026). Its scale-up network uses PCIe switches instead of XeLink but remains a load/store fabric. Porting SyclKittens to it would require validating the operand layouts and prefetch parameters and adapting the communication schedules to the new topology.

2.3. What Raw-SYCL Agents Implement

We inspect the cold-iteration GEMM kernels in §4 to identify which matrix and communication methods raw-SYCL agents implement. In single-GPU bfloat16 (BF16) GEMM, Sonnet and Haiku produce correct kernels that stage operands in SLM without using XMX. Their best correct kernels reach only 5.7%5.7\% and 1.6%1.6\% of Intel’s tuned oneDNN baseline. Opus builds an XMX pipeline from SPIR-V operations, including a Dot Product Accumulate Systolic (DPAS) matrix instruction, 2-D block loads, a BB operand in the interleaved VNNI layout that DPAS requires, and prefetch. However, its thread groups do not coordinate prefetching and repeatedly request the same operand tiles. Its best correct kernel reaches 57.5%57.5\% of that baseline. oneDNN generates Intel GPU assembly through nGEN (oneDNN Project, 2025a) and selects GEMM strategies from a tuned kernel database (oneDNN Project, 2025b). The comparison is therefore against oneDNN’s assembly-generating implementation.

In the distributed GEMM task, input matrix AA is row-sharded, BB is replicated, and every GPU must return the full C=A​BC=AB. A kernel can gather AA before computing the full output, or compute its local rows of CC and then gather the output.

All nine raw-SYCL cold-iteration trials produce correct kernels, but the models combine these choices differently. Haiku computes local output rows but uses vector fused multiply-add (FMA) operations. Sonnet uses XMX but gathers the input and computes the full output on every GPU. Opus uses XMX and overlaps copies across compute and copy queues, but keeps the same replicated-compute decomposition and ignores the MDFI/XeLink topology. Across these trials, no raw-SYCL candidate combines local-output computation, XMX, and topology-aware communication. The best reaches 42.3%42.3\% of our frozen, co-measured, topology-aware SyclKittens hand reference.

These kernels show that access to matrix instructions and peer memory leaves operand coordination and work distribution to the kernel author. SyclKittens encodes operand layouts, cooperative cache prefetch, and topology-aware communication as reusable operations. Programmers and coding agents use those operations while choosing tile shapes, prefetch ownership and distance, and the distribution of computation. Section 3 defines these operations, and §4 evaluates their effect on agent-written kernels.

3. SyclKittens

SyclKittens is a header-only C++ tile programming model for Intel GPUs. Kernels declare typed register or shared-memory tiles, address tensors through global layouts, and express dataflow through tile movement, matrix and reduction operations, and synchronization. The backend lowers these operations to SYCL or SPIR-V and selects their physical lane mappings. Programmers retain C++ control flow and direct access to SYCL or SPIR-V intrinsics. Distributed layouts, peer memory, and GPU-resident synchronization extend the same programming model across a node.

The Intel-specific operations encode matrix operand layouts and packing, cooperative cache prefetch, and topology-aware communication. Tile shape, prefetch ownership and distance, and work distribution remain programmable. In the cumulative single-GPU GEMM ablation, changes to operand layouts, prefetch, and workload-specific schedules raise the geometric mean from 37.4%37.4\% to 96.3%96.3\% of tuned oneDNN. The distributed movement ablation reaches 8282–90%90\% of communication-free GEMM throughput across twelve GPUs. §3.1 defines the interface. §3.2 and §3.3 explain operand layouts, packing, and cooperative prefetch, and §3.4 describes communication within a node.

3.1. Tile Interface

The register-tile type rt<T,M,N,layout,shape> represents a logical M×NM{\times}N two-dimensional array of elements of type T. The layout parameter selects row- or column-major organization, while shape selects a static physical base tile. The GEMM ablation compares 16×1616{\times}16 and 32×3232{\times}32 base tiles; rectangular shapes are also supported. Sub-tile coordinates address rectangular regions within a tile and support cooperative prefetch in §3.3. Bulk rectangular movement and matrix or reduction operations are shared with ThunderKittens. Kernels choose the ordering of load, compute, and store stages over workgroup tiles.

A Global Layout (GL) pairs a device-memory pointer with logical batch, depth, row, and column dimensions. Tile movement operations use its coordinates rather than computing byte offsets in each kernel. A Parallel Global Layout (PGL) (Sul et al., 2025) extends this coordinate space across devices. Additional API and lowering details appear in Appendix B.

3.2. Matrix Operand Layouts and Packing

SyclKittens maps logical row- and column-major tiles onto linear vectors along the SIMD direction, using the 16-lane subgroups that XMX consumes. This differs from matrix fragments distributed across a 32-lane warp in ThunderKittens’ NVIDIA mapping. Fixing the subgroup width at 16 avoids a 32-to-16 operand reorganization inherited from that mapping. For BF16 data, a 32-element tile row matches one 64-byte L1 transaction. A 16-element row consumes only half the cache line, leaving the other half for a later access. The 32×3232{\times}32 base tile therefore halves L1 transactions per 32 values and consumes each line immediately. In the cumulative GEMM ablation, this change raises the geometric mean from 37.4%37.4\% to 68.2%68.2\% of oneDNN (Table 1).

Direct B-operand load and packing.

The SyclKittens API supports two paths from global memory into registers. One stages through a shared tile in SLM, and the other moves directly from a Global Layout into a register tile. ThunderKittens and HipKittens use shared-memory staging followed by ldmatrix or ds_read_b64_tr_b16, respectively. The Intel Max GPU has no equivalent SLM matrix-operand load, so loading a packed B operand from SLM requires multiple ordinary reads. The SyclKittens matrix path instead loads operands directly through L1 cache, avoiding this load sequence and the additional staging and synchronization. For a column-layout right-hand matrix operand B, load_transform lowers to LoadTransformINTEL, a hardware operation that fuses a global 2-D block load with VNNI packing for DPAS. An ordinary load followed by software shuffles is measurably slower; Appendix B reports the packing implementation and its effect.

3.3. Cooperative Cache Prefetch

SyclKittens separates operand delivery into a prefetch phase and a demand phase. prefetch_load issues a 2-D prefetch hint that warms L1 cache without writing the tile’s registers. A later 2-D demand load transfers the cached operands into subgroup registers. This split allows kernels to prefetch future operands while computing with the current tiles, without allocating a shared-memory staging buffer.

prefetch_load_coop takes sub-tile offsets that identify the operand region to prefetch. Kernels assign these offsets to computing subgroups and choose the prefetch distance. The operation provides partial-tile prefetch; the schedule determines ownership and lookahead.

In the cumulative GEMM ablation (Table 1), selective subgroup-masked prefetch raises the geometric mean to 88.8%88.8\% of oneDNN. Loop unrolling and snake traversal, which keeps neighboring workgroups within a compact L2 reuse region, raise it to 91.0%91.0\%. The masked schedule still warms shared operand regions more than once. With partial-tile de-duplication, each subgroup prefetches a disjoint region of the shared operands using the sub-tile coordinates from §3.1. This ownership assignment warms each shared cache region once and raises the mean to 96.2%96.2\%. A final per-shape selection of prefetch distance closes the sequence at 96.3%96.3\% of oneDNN. Appendix D reports the protocol, errors, and per-shape results for this GEMM ablation.

3.4. Topology-Aware GPU Communication

make_pgl combines per-device GLs and peer pointers, and pgl.dev_ptrs[peer] exposes remote high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to ordinary kernel loads and stores. The GPUs share a SYCL context, allowing kernels to dereference peer pointers directly.

GPUs synchronize through peer-visible counters without returning to the host. After writing peer memory, the writing GPU publishes completion with a system-scope release atomic (sycl::atomic_ref). The reading GPU waits with a system-scope acquire atomic. Observing the matching release makes the preceding writes visible to that GPU. signal, wait, and barrier_all implement this protocol.

The topology API groups adjacent stacks into GPU packages with topo::group_pvc and assigns transfer ownership with topo::plan_all_gather. A hierarchical gather sends each shard over XeLink once per remote package, then replicates it to the partner stack over MDFI. This reduces repeated XeLink crossings relative to a flat gather.

PGL permits both kernel-driven peer access and explicit copy-engine transfers. Kernels choose how to divide computation and schedule these transfers. Table 2 holds the GEMM core fixed and varies input-gather schedules to isolate communication changes. Each GPU gathers the missing rows of AA and computes the full CC. The agent study in §4 also explores computing local rows of CC and then gathering the output.

The topology-aware pipeline achieves 2.15×2.15\times and 1.42×1.42\times the end-to-end distributed-GEMM throughput of the flat gather pipeline at the smaller and larger shapes, respectively. The same primitives support collectives and ring attention. Appendices H, I, and J report full sweeps.

4. Controlled Coding-Agent Evaluation

We ask how encoded methods affect agent-written kernel performance, when example kernels help, and how execution feedback improves kernels started from scratch or from a correct implementation. We evaluate Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, and Haiku 4.5 on single-GPU GEMM, distributed GEMM, and causal grouped-query attention (GQA), varying programming context and feedback under a fixed call budget. The SyclKittens contexts supply its complete interface, including cooperative prefetch, but not the co-designed kernels or tuned schedules evaluated in §3. Tables 3 and 4 report controlled endpoints. Figure 3 separately compares selected controlled and co-designed kernels in absolute throughput.

4.1. Experimental Design

Automated harness and tasks.

Our fully automated Claude Code harness evaluates Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, and Haiku 4.5 on 409634096^{3} BF16 GEMM on one GPU, row-sharded 614436144^{3} all-gather GEMM on 12 GPUs, and causal GQA at B=1B{=}1, H=32H{=}32, HK​V=8H_{KV}{=}8, N=2048N{=}2048, and D=128D{=}128.

Programming contexts.

Raw supplies Intel SYCL/SPIR-V documentation. SyclKittens adds headers and API documentation. SyclKittens + examples additionally supplies task-specific kernel source code. For single-GPU GEMM, the examples are ThunderKittens and HipKittens GEMMs. For distributed GEMM, the context also adds a two-GPU SyclKittens all-reduce that shows Intel peer access but not an all-gather GEMM or 12-GPU schedule. For GQA, it adds two HipKittens GQA kernels. None provides an Intel implementation of the target kernel.

Hardware access and launch control.

All contexts permit direct SYCL/SPIR-V intrinsics and forbid oneAPI joint_matrix. All GQA conditions use a byte-identical raw-pointer harness and candidate function signature. Candidates control launch geometry and submissions in every context. Every GQA condition also forbids ESIMD, a separate Intel-specific SIMD programming model that neither raw SYCL nor SyclKittens builds on. We exclude Triton-XPU as a context because it changes both the code generator and programming interface, confounding the comparison. It appears instead as an autotuned performance baseline in §5.2.

Replicates and scope.

Each model-context pair receives three independent starts in both single-shot and cold-iterative evaluation. Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku are one vendor’s large, mid-size, and small tiers, chosen to span capability. We measure how programming context affects generated kernels under a fixed harness and call budget.

Feedback and selection.

We use a custom Claude Code harness rather than the mini-SWE-agent implementation used by ParallelKernelBench (Chan et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024). Both protocols use compilation, correctness, and performance feedback, while ours fixes condition-specific staged files and one evaluator. In single-shot runs, agents can inspect and edit staged files but cannot compile or execute candidates. Cold iterative starts from the context’s blank task stub and receives at most 20 evaluator calls. Warm iterative starts from an eligible single-shot kernel, retains that source as checkpoint 0, and receives the same feedback budget. Under feedback, the harness retains the fastest candidate. After development, we grade the selected candidate on five unseen seeds, with inputs and results withheld from the agent. Every task-specific correctness criterion must hold on every seed.

Performance reporting.

Only correct kernels receive performance scores, and peak@3 is the fastest held-out-correct result among the three starts. Single-GPU single-shot and cold-iterative throughput uses a fixed 197.5-TFLOP/s oneDNN baseline reached through the torch.mm dispatch on Intel XPU. Warm-iterative results use oneDNN co-measured with checkpoint 0 and the final kernel on the assigned GPU. Distributed throughput uses our frozen, co-measured SyclKittens hand reference, which gathers the input with a topology-aware schedule and computes the full output on every GPU. GQA uses native PyTorch XPU SDPA with enable_gqa=True and is_causal=True, co-measured on the same GPU and trial without importing IPEX. Figure 1(b) instead reports median best-so-far trajectories against co-measured oneDNN. Table 3 reports endpoints from correct kernels under the baseline rules above, so the values differ. Appendix C reports exact correctness gates, distributions, and protocol deviations.

4.2. Results

Encoded methods improve single-GPU GEMM

In cold iteration, all nine Opus single-GPU trials are correct, and peak@3 rises from 57.5%57.5\% with Raw to 82.1%82.1\% with SyclKittens and 82.6%82.6\% with SyclKittens + examples. Sonnet also improves from 5.7%5.7\% with Raw to 85.2%85.2\% with SyclKittens. The tile programming model supplies XMX computation, operand layout, and data movement as operations that agents can compose while tuning schedules. Without feedback, SyclKittens raises Opus correctness from 1/3 to 3/3 and peak@3 from 6.6%6.6\% to 63.4%63.4\% on one GPU, while raising distributed GEMM correctness from 0/3 to 2/3.

The median Opus SyclKittens trajectory in Figure 1(b) passes Raw’s final level on the second evaluator call. This measures search efficiency separately from the peak@3 endpoints.

Context effects vary across models and tasks.

All 27 cold-iterative GQA trials are correct, but their peak@3 context ordering changes by model. SyclKittens + examples leads for Opus at 79.5%79.5\%, whereas Raw leads for Sonnet at 18.6%18.6\%, above SyclKittens + examples at 8.8%8.8\% and SyclKittens at 4.6%4.6\%. Haiku remains between 0.7%0.7\% and 1.3%1.3\% across all contexts. The best Sonnet result is below the weakest Opus context at 41.6%41.6\%. Sonnet’s reversal from GEMM to GQA shows that a context’s benefit also depends on the task. Every selected Opus GQA kernel uses XMX through direct subgroup DPAS, so its gain from examples reflects schedule search rather than access to a different low-level mechanism. Full GQA results appear in Appendix C.7.

Example kernels help in some settings.

Without feedback, examples raise Opus peak@3 from 63.4%63.4\% to 81.2%81.2\% on one GPU and from 36.7%36.7\% to 59.4%59.4\% on distributed GEMM, where correctness also rises from 2/3 to 3/3. In cold iteration, Opus reaches about 82%82\% on single-GPU GEMM in both SyclKittens contexts, and Sonnet and Haiku vary by task and protocol. The examples’ measured benefit therefore depends on the model, task, and starting condition.

Agents consistently refine correct kernels.

Warm iterative refinement retains the original correct kernel while feedback improves its schedule. All seven eligible Opus single-GPU GEMM sources and all six Opus GQA sources remain correct and improve, reaching 87.8%87.8\% and 83.4%83.4\% of their respective baselines. All thirteen eligible distributed sources across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku in the two SyclKittens contexts also remain correct and improve. The strongest reaches 106.6%106.6\% of our co-measured reference by computing local output-row shards before gathering the output, avoiding redundant full-GEMM work on every GPU (Appendix C.5).

Source inspection identifies implementation choices.

As §2.3 shows, selected Raw kernels either bypass XMX or fail to coordinate the full operand pipeline. Every context exposes the same SPIR-V and XMX instructions, but the strongest no-feedback Opus kernel in SyclKittens + examples combines mma_AB, 2-D loads, VNNI packing, a 32×3232{\times}32 register base shape, and three-tile prefetch, while the correct single-shot Raw kernel only uses vector FMA. The SyclKittens interface supplies the matrix and movement operations, while the generated kernel chooses the tile shape and prefetch distance. Full source inspection appears in Appendix C.

5. SyclKittens Inference Kernel Suite

Engineers and coding agents co-designed the SyclKittens inference kernel suite. Unlike the autonomous trials in §4, they jointly refine tile shapes, prefetch ownership and distance, and work distribution under correctness and performance checks set by engineers. This section reports the suite’s throughput against tuned vendor paths.

5.1. Experimental Setup

PyTorch 2.10 with IPEX 2.10.10 (Intel Corporation, 2025a) dispatches operator baselines to oneDNN (oneDNN Project, 2024; PyTorch Contributors, 2026), fused SDPA, or oneCCL. Our standalone decode GEMV baseline calls Intel’s optimized oneMKL math library directly through oneapi::mkl::blas::gemm (Intel Corporation, 2025b). Fusion and end-to-end results use torch.compile. For the Triton comparison, we use identical shapes, correctness gates, and measurement windows with Triton-XPU 3.6’s standard GEMM implementation, autotuned.

Every sweep warms up before timing and co-measures each SyclKittens candidate with its baseline in the same thermal window. We report geometric means of per-shape speedups. SyclKittens GEMM requires relative Frobenius error below 0.02. Appendix D reports per-shape data and additional correctness gates.

5.2. Kernel Results

Dense GEMM across shapes and nodes.

The GEMM of §3.3 reaches 96.3%96.3\% of oneDNN in geometric mean across the 27 shapes in Figure 5(a). Across six independently measured nodes at 819238192^{3}, the per-node SyclKittens/oneDNN relative performance ranges from 95.5%95.5\% to 96.3%96.3\%. An interleaved six-node sweep finds that the final cooperative revision exceeds autotuned Triton-XPU 3.6 on all 27 shapes, with 1.087×1.087\times geometric-mean throughput. Appendix D reports the direct comparison, exact tables, Stream-K results, and ablations.

Attention reuses the HipKittens algorithm.

The attention kernel reuses the complete HipKittens dataflow algorithm through the tile interface. For each query tile, the GQA kernel retains HipKittens’ sequence of tiled Q​K⊤QK^{\top}, running-maximum and normalizer updates, output rescaling, and P​VPV accumulation. The dataflow therefore needs no algorithmic change. SyclKittens re-implements its tile operations with Intel’s matrix, movement, and prefetch instructions. Figure 4 reports the resulting MHA and GQA throughput. The GQA baseline dispatches through its MHA path and repeats eight KV heads to match the 32 query heads, so that margin is against a fallback rather than a tuned vendor GQA kernel.

Decode-critical operators.

The remaining SyclKittens kernels outperform their vendor baselines on the operations that dominate autoregressive decode. These operations either run briefly, so launch overhead matters, or stream weights from memory. Fused root mean square layer normalization (RMSNorm) (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019), layer normalization (LayerNorm) (Ba et al., 2016), and RoPE each use one launch. Split-K GEMV matters most because the five M=1M{=}1 Llama projections account for about 64%64\% of per-token decode latency. SyclKittens maps each output-row reduction across cooperating subgroups so the GPU stays occupied as tensor-parallel shards shrink. Figure 5(b) reports these gains before §6.1 measures them inside a full decode loop. Appendices F and G report the full grids.

6. End-to-End Inference

We measure how the kernel gains translate to Llama-3.1-8B inference (Grattafiori and others, 2024) on one GPU and across a node. Composed with torch.compile, SyclKittens improves full-request throughput by 1.59×1.59\times in geometric mean over torch.compile alone on the single-GPU configurations. Across twelve GPUs, SyclKittens also serves a 256K context. That memory-capacity result is separate from the matched-GPU-count speedups below.

6.1. Framework Composition on One GPU

Operator ownership.

We compare SyclKittens composed with torch.compile with torch.compile alone. torch.compile generates Triton for the pointwise, standalone normalization, and epilogue regions it fuses, but graph-breaks at attention on XPU. Across this boundary, SyclKittens supplies a FlashAttention-style kernel (Dao et al., 2022), fused Q/K rotary, fused QKV projection, and residual-plus-RMSNorm fusion. The kernels are exposed as PyTorch custom operations and installed by replacing the Llama decoder layer at runtime; HuggingFace source and model.generate() remain unchanged.

Prefill and decode.

Figure 6 reports Llama-3.1-8B inference throughput over four batch sizes and six context lengths. Each point times one synchronized, deterministic model.generate() request with up to 128 new tokens. The reported full-request rate counts batch-wide prompt tokens plus the generated sequence length of one stream, as defined in Appendix K.4. Geometric means use the 21 configurations in which both systems fit. The composed path improves prefill by 1.22×1.22\times, decode by 1.65×1.65\times, and full-request prefill-plus-decode throughput by 1.59×1.59\times (range 1.291.29–1.98×1.98\times). Prefill gains grow with context because the SyclKittens FlashAttention-style kernel avoids the baseline’s quadratic score materialization; decode gains come from eliminating launches around that attention boundary and from the projection path in §5.2. Neither system uses SYCL Graph, Intel’s equivalent of CUDA graph capture, in these measurements.

6.2. Node-Scale Composition

At node scale, decode performance depends on communication latency. In the evaluated batch-one decode, each tensor-parallel all-reduce carries one 4096-element BF16 hidden vector (8 KiB), so launch, process, and synchronization latency matter more than peak bulk bandwidth. SyclKittens keeps all GPUs in one process and one shared SYCL context; a host thread launches each GPU’s stream, and inline peer movement with system-scope device barriers keeps Python and cross-process dispatch off the per-token path.

Inference-scale collectives.

At 24 KiB, SyclKittens outperforms oneCCL on all four collectives by 1.811.81–3.31×3.31\times. Reduce-scatter reaches 2.20×2.20\times at 0.19 MiB and remains 1.10×1.10\times faster at 96 MiB. Destination-split all-to-all reaches 3.49×3.49\times at 1.5 MiB and remains 1.20×1.20\times faster at 96 MiB. At that largest payload, oneCCL leads all-reduce and all-gather, where SyclKittens reaches 0.94×0.94\times and 0.92×0.92\times of oneCCL.

Context-parallel attention.

Long contexts also require splitting attention across GPUs. When the full KV cache fits in each GPU’s HBM, SyclKittens gathers it once and executes one flash pass. When it does not, a ring rotates one KV shard per step and merges the online softmax state. Copy-engine overlap leads the blocking PyTorch sendrecv ring at every context we measure, by 1.211.21–2.46×2.46\times (Figure 7(a)). At 49K total tokens, the overlapped non-causal ring reaches 60.7 TFLOP/s per GPU, versus 42.0 for the blocking baseline. All-gather exceeds the sequential ring across the measured context sweep when the gathered KV cache fits in HBM; the ring provides the memory-scaling policy beyond that point.

6.3. Multi-GPU Decode

The Llama decoder composes tensor-parallel projections and inline all-reduces with context-parallel attention. Figure 7(b) shows that, at matched GPU count, the SyclKittens decode path outperforms the oneCCL-based path at every context, by up to 2.91×2.91\times at 32K on four GPUs. This comparison includes both the source-partitioned collective and SyclKittens’s single-process execution model. The standalone results above measure complete collective calls without the surrounding decoder, while retaining each implementation’s process model.

The best layout changes with context. Flat four-way tensor parallelism wins through 32K. At 64K and 128K, TP​2×CP​3\mathrm{TP}2{\times}\mathrm{CP}3 uses six GPUs to shard the growing KV scan, and at 256K, TP​4×CP​3\mathrm{TP}4{\times}\mathrm{CP}3 uses all twelve GPUs and serves at 73.3 ms/token. The last point is a capacity result, since the two-GPU tuned oneCCL path is out of memory there and the SyclKittens configuration uses more GPUs. Appendices I, J, and K provide per-shape tables, integration and correctness details, per-layer collective costs, the ring-attention step breakdown, timing-tail summaries, and layout sweeps.

7. Conclusion

SyclKittens is a tile programming model for Intel GPUs that provides matrix operand layouts, cooperative cache prefetch, and topology-aware GPU communication as reusable operations. With SyclKittens, the strongest coding agent in our study writes a faster single-GPU GEMM kernel than in raw SYCL under the same task and feedback budget. Through engineer-agent co-design, SyclKittens also supports a kernel suite that approaches oneDNN on GEMM and outperforms SDPA with IPEX on causal MHA. In Llama-3.1-8B inference, it outperforms torch.compile on one GPU and the oneCCL-based decode path on multiple GPUs.

A study of human experts in raw SYCL and SyclKittens would test whether the same interface also reduces expert development effort. Once Crescent Island is available, we can test whether SyclKittens’s encoded compute methods transfer while its node schedules are retuned for a PCIe-based fabric (Mohan and Jiang, 2026).

As coding agents take on kernel development for new accelerators, our results suggest that the programming interface should carry each architecture’s methods. Agents then start from known-good building blocks and spend their search on workload-specific policies.
