Appendix overview

These appendices separate outputs of the controlled-agent studies from the co-designed SyclKittens suite. Each experiment identifies its library baseline or author-built reference, along with its measurement and aggregation protocol.

Shared measurement protocol.

Unless stated otherwise, single-GPU experiments activate one stack per GPU package and leave its sibling idle. Every reported configuration passes the section-specific reference check before timing. Warmup, repetition, aggregation, and byte/FLOP conventions are stated with each experiment. Displayed measurements are rounded; ratios use the unrounded values.

Appendix A Hardware and Programming-Interface Map

This section defines the terminology and programming interfaces used in the main paper’s Background and Motivation and SyclKittens sections. The cross-vendor table aligns functions; implementation costs remain platform-specific. A node contains six GPU packages, each with two stacks connected by MDFI, the load/store stack-to-stack interconnect. XeLink connects the GPU packages all-to-all through two independent stack planes, even and odd.

A.1. Measured Fabric Behavior

We characterize the two communication tiers on the same 12-stack Intel Max GPU node used in the main evaluation. Direct peer kernels issue contiguous remote loads or stores through pointers in one shared SYCL context. The collective measurements use five warmups followed by 15 timed iterations and report the median; the two-stack all-reduce bandwidth uses 2​(N−1)​S/(N​t)2(N-1)S/(Nt), while distributed-GEMM speedups use raw elapsed-time ratios. These conventions are reported separately because they are not interchangeable estimates of a physical link rate.

The topology-aware gather sends each source stripe over XeLink once to one landing stack per remote GPU package, then replicates it to the partner stack over MDFI. This halves XeLink egress relative to every stack fetching every remote stripe. Same-plane transfers can occupy both XeLink planes concurrently; cross-plane transfers additionally consume the six MDFI links, which lowers the number of independent flows the node can sustain. Kernels can issue peer loads and stores over both fabrics. For explicit copies, the Intel Max GPU also exposes per-link copy engines; simply offloading a naive all-pairs copy does not reproduce the bandwidth of a topology-aware schedule.

A.2. Intel Programming-Interface Taxonomy

The interfaces available on the same hardware differ in how much schedule structure they expose. SYCL joint_matrix is a portable matrix API. It leaves operand layout and lowering to the implementation, but does not expose the complete 2-D movement and prefetch schedule used here. ESIMD provides Intel-specific explicit-SIMD control and is the substrate for larger template libraries such as XeTLA. Direct SPIR-V built-ins expose individual XMX and 2-D block operations but leave their legal and profitable composition to each kernel author.

SyclKittens application kernels use a compact tile programming model whose backend lowers to the same Intel SPIR-V operations. The backend defines the SIMD16/XMX contract, physical register layout, VNNI operand transform, cache-based 2-D movement, and partial-tile prefetch operations. Kernels choose prefetch ownership and distance. The controlled study therefore evaluates a stable tile programming model with an explicitly architecture-specific lowering.

Appendix B Tile Language Mechanisms

B.1. Realization Details

Prior work describes the initial SYCL port of ThunderKittens (Jiang et al., 2026). Our baseline for this port compiled and linked on Intel Max GPU but passed only 570 of 1032 unit tests (55%). Six root causes account for every failure. With these fixes, the library used by the measured kernels passed all 1032 unit tests. We describe these fixes, the added operations and performance primitives, the prefetch API behind §3.3, and the measured SLM limits that motivate the L1 operand path.

B.1.1. Critical Correctness Fixes

We identified six distinct root causes accounting for all 462 test failures (Table 8). The largest groups are shared-to-register layout, incomplete vector operations, and row reduction. The failures include NVIDIA warp-32 and CUDA-shuffle assumptions that do not survive the move to Intel Max GPU’s SIMD16 execution model, XMX packing errors, and incomplete conversion or reduction paths. Each failure mode requires a separate fix.

Fix 4 also resolves an interaction with the VNNI hardware transform load (§B.1.2). Incorrect hmma81616 operand marshalling made transform-loaded operands appear corrupt, prompting a temporary switch from LoadTransformINTEL to LoadINTEL. Once contiguous operand packing and K-split accumulator chaining corrected hmma81616, restoring LoadTransformINTEL retained 1032/1032 correctness and removed software VNNI repacking.

B.1.2. Performance Primitives and New Operations

Three PVC-specific primitives affect the measured kernels. move_local<T> annotates SLM pointers with __attribute__((opencl_local)) (§B.1.4). For rt_16x32 float tiles, the 2D block-load path splits a BlockCount=2 request into two BlockCount=1 loads to remain within Intel Max GPU’s 64-byte hardware load width. The __spirv_Subgroup2DBlockLoadTransformINTEL path performs the GEMM B-operand VNNI repack during the load. Combined with the corrected hmma81616, restoring this transform raises single-GPU 819238192^{3} GEMM throughput from 106 to 147 TFLOP/s, a 39% gain over the regular-load path with software repacking.

The kernels also use three groups of tile-language operations. load_part and store_part with a position parameter (the split-D strategy that processes D=128D{=}128 as two D=64D{=}64 passes within register budget); make_causal with partial-tile support for causal masking at non-aligned tile boundaries; and mul::reduce and min::reduce completions, since upstream ThunderKittens only exposed sum and max reductions.

B.1.3. Prefetch API

SyclKittens separates cache warming from the register load that consumes a tile.

⬇
prefetch_load(tile, global, next);
prefetch_load_coop(tile, global, next, {row, col});
load(tile, global, next);

prefetch_load emits Intel 2-D block-prefetch instructions for the base regions implied by the register-tile shape. It warms L1 but does not write the destination registers; the later load performs the XMX-compatible 2-D block load. The prefetch is therefore a performance hint, not an asynchronous copy whose completion is required for correctness.

prefetch_load_coop exposes ownership within a workgroup. One call warms a single 16-column, 8-row, two-block region at the supplied raw row and column offset. The GEMM schedule assigns disjoint offsets to its computing subgroups, so every shared operand region is warmed once while all subgroups continue to issue matrix work. The destination argument supplies tile shape and coordinate types only; it is not modified.

Cache-based staging.

This interface is distinct from two shared memory mechanisms often also called prefetching. SLM staging copies global data into programmer-managed local memory before a synchronized load, while SLM fetch-ahead combines a load, local-memory store, and named-barrier handoff. The measured Intel Max GPU path uses neither. Hardware 2-D prefetch places data in the configurable 512 KB L1, and each consumer later loads its own register tile. This cache-centric split preserves ordinary load semantics while allowing the cooperative ownership policy in §3.3 to remove redundant warming.

B.1.4. Measured Limits of SLM Operand Staging

Two measured costs keep shared local memory (SLM) off the operand-staging path on Intel Max GPU, namely narrow matrix-operand loads and compiler overhead from generic address-space qualification.

A- and B-operand costs.

Intel Max GPU has no SLM matrix load (ldmatrix equivalent). Loading an XMX B-operand (16×1616{\times}16 bf16) from SLM requires ∼\sim64 individual reads vs. a single LoadTransformINTEL from HBM. Multiple SLM-based attention-kernel attempts ran an order of magnitude below the HBM-native path (the measured SLM B-operand variant reached 2.32.3–3.03.0 TFLOPS against tens of TFLOPS for the HBM path) because that 64:164{:}1 read penalty compounds with the compiler overhead below.

Address-space qualification matters.

ThunderKittens’ st<> shared-tile type stores SLM base pointers as uintptr_t, which Intel’s IGC compiler treats as generic address space. IGC emits approximately 1,400 runtime disambiguation IR operations, adding more cost than the SLM staging removes. Typed local_accessor<T> or multi_ptr<T,local_space> fixes this, and SyclKittens’s move_local<T> of §B.1.2 applies the equivalent annotation. Address-space annotations do not remove the 64:164{:}1 read-count difference above, which motivates the direct operand path used by the measured kernels.

Appendix C Controlled Coding-Agent Studies

The controlled studies cover single-GPU BF16 GEMM, causal grouped-query attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023), and 12-GPU all-gather BF16 GEMM under single-shot and independent cold-iterative feedback protocols. All three tasks use Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku in the single-shot and cold-iterative arms. Warm-iterative follow-ups use Opus on single-GPU GEMM and GQA and all eligible model–context sources in the two SyclKittens contexts on distributed GEMM. They seed feedback with held-out-correct single-shot sources, separating blank-start search from warm refinement. The task, programming context, evaluator, and budget were fixed before measurement.

C.1. Shared Controls

Across all three tasks, each model–context pair receives three independent starts for both single-shot and cold-iterative evaluation. The evaluated models are Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, and Haiku 4.5. Each task uses three nested programming contexts. Raw provides Intel SYCL/SPIR-V documentation but no SyclKittens. The SyclKittens context adds its headers and API documentation without a target-kernel implementation. That documentation covers the whole interface, including prefetch_load_coop and its region-offset argument, so every mechanism the co-designed kernels use is available to the agent. The example context is SyclKittens + examples, whose task-specific contents are specified below. Every condition permits direct SYCL/SPIR-V intrinsics and forbids oneAPI joint_matrix, its matrix headers, and its namespace.

The agent runtime is Claude Code 2.1.214, not mini-SWE-agent. Our custom harness shares ParallelKernelBench’s edit–evaluate–refine structure (Chan et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024). ParallelKernelBench uses mini-SWE-agent, a repository-rooted shell, and a budget of 20 model calls. Our harness fixes condition-specific staged files and programming context and limits feedback to 20 evaluator calls. After development, the selected candidate must pass five unseen correctness seeds; no held-out input or result is exposed to the agent.

Single-shot agents can read, search, and edit staged task files but have no shell, compiler, evaluator, benchmark, network, or external repository access. Cold-iterative agents additionally receive at most 20 calls to one fixed compile–correctness–performance evaluator. Warm-iterative agents begin from an eligible held-out-correct single-shot source as checkpoint 0. Replicates start independently, no source transfers between trials, and the agent never sees the five held-out seeds. Under feedback, the harness retains the fastest development-correct candidate.

C.2. Single-GPU Task

Every trial implements M=N=K=4096M{=}N{=}K{=}4096 BF16 GEMM with FP32 accumulation. SyclKittens + examples adds fixed ThunderKittens and HipKittens GEMM implementations. All conditions target the same GPU, compiler toolchain, output contract, and evaluator.

Protocol.

Final correctness requires all five held-out seeds to pass. Performance is throughput divided by the fixed 197.5-TFLOP/s tuned oneDNN baseline, reached through the torch.mm dispatch on Intel XPU and measured on the same GPU. The main paper reports every model separately for single-shot and cold-iterative trials and summarizes Opus warm-iterative refinement; the full multi-model distributed warm-iterative campaign appears below. Both performance summaries use only correct trials, because the median and range describe reliability among held-out-correct trials, whereas peak@3 is the maximum held-out-correct result from the three independent trials.

C.3. Single-GPU Complete Controlled Results

Table 10 gives the ranges omitted from Table 3 in the main paper. A dash means that no trial passed all five held-out seeds.

C.4. Single-GPU Warm-Iterative Refinement

The retained Raw Opus source rises from 6.47% to 14.24%. Raw has one eligible source, so its final median and maximum in Table 3 are both 14.2%. The matched follow-up begins from the six held-out-correct Opus sources in the two SyclKittens contexts. Together with Raw, all seven Opus sources remain correct and improve under paired grading.

Warm-iterative feedback improves every source. The two SyclKittens contexts reach effectively tied frontiers (87.83% in SyclKittens and 87.71% in SyclKittens + examples), while examples raise the final median from 70.46% to 86.51%. The Raw source improves from 6.47% to 14.24%.

C.5. Distributed All-Gather GEMM Studies

The distributed task asks each agent to implement a complete 12-GPU, row-sharded BF16 all-gather GEMM at M=N=K=6144M{=}N{=}K{=}6144. Each GPU initially owns 512 rows of dense random AA; BB is replicated; and every GPU must produce the full replicated BF16 C=A​BC{=}AB with FP32 accumulation. Candidates implement the complete communication-and-compute path. The timed interval includes both components, and throughput is reported per GPU as 2​M​K​N/t2MKN/t.

Task-specific context.

SyclKittens + examples adds a ThunderKittens H100 BF16 GEMM, a HipKittens AMD BF16 GEMM, and a two-GPU SyclKittens all-reduce. The GEMM examples target NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. The all-reduce demonstrates Intel peer access, but none of the three programs implements an all-gather GEMM, a 12-GPU schedule, or the topology-aware hand baseline, so the agent must compose the communication and compute path. All other treatment and tool controls follow the shared protocol above.

Correctness, timing, and anti-amortization.

Correctness requires finite sampled output, relative L2 error below 0.03 on all five held-out seeds, and agreement on every GPU. Timing uses a 2-second power warmup, five explicit warmups, and the median of 15 complete operations. Before every warmup and scored invocation, the harness regenerates a distinct deterministic AA epoch outside the timed interval, then verifies the final epoch on all 12 outputs. A negative control that deliberately reuses gathered data fails this gate with post-timing relative L2 error 1.38, whereas valid raw-SYCL and SyclKittens candidates pass it; generated code therefore cannot remove communication by retaining gathered scratch across calls.

Performance is normalized to the co-measured topology-aware hand baseline on the assigned node. This campaign-local reference gathers AA and then computes the full CC on every GPU. It uses the evaluator’s deterministic input distribution and the frozen masked-prefetch build, rather than the random-normal cooperative-prefetch configuration in Table 49. In the single-shot campaign, the hand baseline spans 126.7–131.0 TFLOPS across six nodes, with a 128.9-TFLOPS median. The tuned vendor library path combines oneCCL all-gather with PyTorch’s oneDNN GEMM. Timed end to end, it spans 128.9–144.3 TFLOPS, with a 134.9-TFLOPS median. That value is unrelated to the numerically identical SyclKittens GEMM-only value in Table 49. The matched factor sweep in Table 50 reproduces both SyclKittens operating points and attributes the difference primarily to the evaluator-versus-random-normal operand distribution, not to agent tuning. Table 12 reports only held-out-correct trials and uses the node-matched hand baseline as its denominator.

Model-stratified result.

Single-shot effects depend on the model. Examples raise the Opus frontier from 36.7% to 59.4% and the Sonnet median from 0.3% to 34.2%, whereas Haiku remains below 1% in both SyclKittens contexts. Four of Raw’s five correct kernels also remain below 0.5%. No generated kernel exceeds the hand baseline or tuned oneCCL library path.

Cold-iterative protocol.

The feedback study keeps the task, programming contexts, evaluator, and three replicates per model and condition fixed. Each replicate begins independently from its treatment’s initial task template, with no candidate code transferred from the single-shot study or another replicate. Agents receive at most 20 calls to the fixed compile-correctness-performance evaluator. The fastest development-correct candidate is then graded on the five held-out seeds.

Cold feedback changes Sonnet most, whose two SyclKittens contexts reach 50.9% and 41.1%, compared with its 25.8% Raw frontier. Opus changes modestly from Raw, and Haiku remains low-throughput in both SyclKittens contexts.

Distributed warm-iterative refinement.

Warm-iterative refinement starts from every eligible held-out-correct single-shot source in the two SyclKittens contexts, namely six in SyclKittens and seven in SyclKittens + examples, spanning five Opus, six Sonnet, and two Haiku trials. All 13 sources remain held-out correct and improve. Table 14 reports each paired result relative to the node-matched hand baseline.

The 106.6%106.6\% source improves the distributed algorithm rather than the dense GEMM microkernel. It computes each GPU’s CC row shard from the local AA shard and replicated BB, then performs a topology-aware all-gather of CC. Because this task has N=KN{=}K, gathering C⁡(M×N)C\,(M{\times}N) moves the same BF16 tensor volume as gathering A⁡(M×K)A\,(M{\times}K), but the transformation reduces aggregate GEMM work from 12 full products to one full product partitioned across 12 GPUs. It remains a valid result, because the fixed harness regenerates AA before every invocation, waits both queue sets, and verifies the full replicated CC on every GPU for all five held-out seeds.

Every eligible source improves. Median paired gains are 5.4 and 5.5 percentage points in SyclKittens and SyclKittens + examples, respectively, and one SyclKittens Opus source reaches 106.6% of hand (136.311 versus 127.91 TFLOP/s). Because eligibility produces different source populations, these results establish per-source refinement rather than a balanced comparison between contexts.

Engineer-agent co-design.

The controlled sources above remain frozen for attribution. A matched Box–Muller comparison found that the SyclKittens + examples kernel reached 131.616 TFLOP/s, exceeding the 128.545 of our initial refinement of a SyclKittens kernel. We restarted from the unchanged SyclKittens + examples kernel and retained it as the incumbent under a monotonic promotion rule. The selected refinement retains its DPAS core and cross-package route, then applies cyclic MDFI band order with a two/four split over the compute/copy queues. It reaches 125.724 TFLOP/s versus 123.839 for the incumbent in a new four-node random-normal study, with a 1.007×1.007\times node-first paired ratio that sits within run-to-run variation (Table 48). In this workflow, agents expand the algorithm family, engineers retain the strongest validated source as the incumbent, and joint tuning is accepted only under a common correctness and performance gate.

C.6. Single-GPU Mechanism Inspection

The single-shot Opus frontier in SyclKittens + examples is replicate r2. Its selected source declares a 32×3232{\times}32 register base shape, presents B in the VNNI-compatible column layout, sets the K-tile prefetch distance to three, uses 2-D loads, and reaches DPAS through mma_AB. It reaches 160.4 TFLOP/s, or 81.2% of the fixed oneDNN baseline. The cold-iterative frontiers in the remaining columns also use mma_AB, 2-D loads, and VNNI-compatible B, but select different schedules.

Raw cold frontiers are 57.5% for Opus, 5.7% for Sonnet, and 1.6% for Haiku. Direct SPIR-V/XMX access is available in every condition. The generated sources differ in their tiling and operand-delivery implementations.

C.7. Three-Model Grouped-Query Attention

We evaluate Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku on causal GQA at B=1B{=}1, H=32H{=}32, HK​V=8H_{KV}{=}8, N=2048N{=}2048, and D=128D{=}128 under a corrected equal-ownership protocol. The Sonnet and Haiku extension changes only the model alias. Its five frozen task inputs are byte-identical to the Opus campaign, including the raw-pointer harness with SHA-256 bdd6bd8ff88d83c29b0f6a4655268407906a2fd63e9179cce173935db143b9c. Raw, SyclKittens, and SyclKittens + examples use that harness and the same candidate function signature. Every candidate owns its launch geometry, work-group and subgroup mapping, and submissions. ESIMD is forbidden in every condition because it is a separate Intel-specific SIMD programming model that neither raw SYCL nor SyclKittens builds on. Direct SPIR-V subgroup matrix and 2-D block-I/O intrinsics remain available. Raw provides Intel SYCL/SPIR-V documentation, SyclKittens adds its headers, and SyclKittens + examples additionally provides two HipKittens causal-GQA kernels for AMD GPUs rather than an Intel implementation.

Each of the 27 cold-iterative trials independently starts from a no-op condition stub and receives at most 20 evaluator calls. The 27 single-shot trials use the same frozen inputs without evaluator feedback. Correctness requires finite output, relative L2 error below 0.05, and elementwise error rate below 0.01 on all five held-out seeds. Performance is normalized by the native PyTorch XPU SDPA baseline co-measured in each trial, with enable_gqa=True and is_causal=True. The baseline process does not import IPEX. The observed cold-iterative baselines range from 73.0 to 85.3 TFLOP/s. The kernel-suite sweep in §E imports IPEX and measures its grouped-head fallback.

Context effects differ by model.

Examples lead for Opus at 79.5%79.5\%, while Raw leads for Sonnet at 18.6%18.6\%, followed by examples at 8.8%8.8\% and SyclKittens at 4.6%4.6\%. Haiku remains between 0.7%0.7\% and 1.3%1.3\% across all contexts. The best Sonnet cell falls below the weakest Opus cell at 41.6%41.6\%. All 27 kernels are correct, so correctness alone would hide this model effect. A pooled context average would also hide the reversal between Opus and Sonnet and is therefore not reported.

The single-shot arms contain 27 infrastructure-valid cells and 23 held-out-correct endpoints. The only incorrect Sonnet or Haiku endpoint is Haiku SyclKittens replicate 1, whose generated candidate fails the build gate. This is a correctness outcome rather than a harness failure.

Opus warm refinement.

The endpoint-seeded warm campaign is separate from the balanced cold grid. It refines the six held-out-correct Opus single-shot sources and does not include Sonnet or Haiku. All six remain correct and improve. Paired gains range from 9.5 to 81.7 percentage points, and the strongest endpoint reaches 71.0 TFLOP/s or 83.4%83.4\% of its co-measured baseline. Unequal eligibility makes these paired refinements rather than a balanced context comparison.

Opus mechanisms and variance.

All nine selected Opus cold-iterative kernels reach XMX through direct SPIR-V subgroup DPAS, and eight also use direct 2-D block I/O. The strongest Raw kernel reaches 42.3 TFLOP/s with transformed 2-D loads and prefetch, while the strongest example-assisted kernel reaches 59.9 TFLOP/s with direct 2-D loads, transposed loads, and prefetch. The selected Opus kernels from SyclKittens and SyclKittens + examples use direct intrinsics rather than SyclKittens register-tile or MMA APIs. The treatment therefore changes the schedules Opus discovers even when the final implementations use the same low-level mechanism family.

The HipKittens examples expose tiled causal-attention algebra and pipelining, but the generated kernels are Intel implementations. The strongest Opus result translates that structure into PVC DPAS and cache-prefetch operations, while the other two example-assisted replicates do not reproduce the same schedule. Only the strongest of the three example-assisted Opus starts exceeds Raw’s cold-iteration peak.

C.8. Data Quality and Protocol Deviations

The deviations below do not alter the planned balance of the single-shot or cold-iterative comparisons. Warm-iterative analyses remain paired because eligibility determines their source populations.

The accompanying artifact retains prompts, programming contexts, generated sources, agent interactions, development evaluations, selected candidates, and held-out logs for independent inspection.

C.9. AI Use in SyclKittens development

The autonomous controlled study is distinct from the engineer-agent suite. Intel hardware experts helped design the programming model. Engineers and coding agents collaborated on implementation, call-site integration, variant generation, and tuning. Engineers owned the experiments and correctness and performance acceptance. Generated code entered the suite only after compilation, operation-specific tests, interleaved measurement, and human review, as described by the main-paper AI disclosure.

Appendix D BF16 GEMM

Across the 27-shape evaluation suite, the SyclKittens bf16 GEMM with collaborative de-duplicated prefetch achieves 0.963×0.963\times oneDNN in geometric-mean throughput. Measurements use bf16 output, shape-adaptive launch policies, within-trial co-measurement, and six-node aggregation.

D.1. Configuration

GEMM FLOPs are 2​M​K​N2MKN for both implementations, so their TFLOPS figures are directly comparable.

D.2. Kernel Implementation and Key Techniques

The GEMM kernel is a single compile-time-templated translation unit built into a callable per-shape module; each shape in the 27-shape evaluation suite is compiled separately.

Data flow (per output tile). Each subgroup owns a BM×BN\mathrm{BM}\times\mathrm{BN} (32×6432{\times}64) fp32 accumulator register tile c_reg and streams the KK dimension in BK=32\mathrm{BK}{=}32 chunks. For each K-step it loads a BM×BK\mathrm{BM}\times\mathrm{BK} bf16 AA tile (row-major) and a BK×BN\mathrm{BK}\times\mathrm{BN} bf16 BB tile (column-major) via 2D block loads, with the VNNI transform applied to B. It issues the DPAS contraction into c_reg and prefetches future AA/BB panels at the configured lookahead distance. After the K loop, c_reg is scaled and stored.

Key techniques
  • •

    Register-resident DPAS tiling. A 32×6432{\times}64 fp32 accumulator per subgroup (falling back to 16×1616{\times}16 register tiles for sub-32 output tiles), bf16 operand tiles, and up to 32 subgroups per work-group keep the systolic array fed. Profiling shows the kernel is DPAS-bound (XVE about 94.5% array-active, L3 bandwidth about 1.3% of peak), so large, well-populated work-groups matter more than additional cache optimization.

  • •

    VNNI 2D block loads. Hardware block-load instructions with the VNNI operand transform deliver bf16 operands to the DPAS unit in their native packed layout, avoiding a local-memory staging round trip.

  • •

    Masked prefetch baseline. Before de-duplication, full-tile A prefetches are issued when sg_id % 5 != 0, and full-tile B prefetches are issued when sg_id & 8 != 0. This selective schedule reaches 88.8%88.8\% of oneDNN. Loop unrolling and snake traversal then raise the geometric mean to 91.0%91.0\%.

  • •

    Snake-curve group swizzle. Work-group tiles are traversed in an L2-friendly super-stack order, with the swizzle width fixed per shape (4 at 204832048^{3}, 16 at 307233072^{3}/819238192^{3}, 4 at 12288312288^{3}/16384316384^{3}, 8 for other square shapes, 8 for all rectangular shapes) from a full snake-width sweep. A guard falls back to linear indexing for non-aligned grids, and grid padding with an early-return bounds check (returning when a work-group’s row or column tile index exceeds the grid) prevents tile skips and output corruption on non-divisible snake grids.

  • •

    Collaborative de-duplicated prefetch. The partial-tile policy assigns every subgroup a disjoint slice of the shared 256×32256{\times}32 A and 32×25632{\times}256 B workgroup panels. Each panel byte is warmed once per K-step, rather than once per consuming subgroup; the prologue uses the same assignment.

  • •

    Shape-adaptive lookahead. De-duplication reduces explicit prefetch traffic by about 3.6×3.6\times and enables deeper lookahead, namely distance 2 for all squares and mostly distance 3 for rectangles, with measured distance-1 and distance-2 exceptions. The retained masked baseline instead uses distance 1 for K>4096K>4096 and distance 2 otherwise.

  • •

    K-loop unroll (32-way). Exposing 32 K-iterations to the compiler overlaps loads with MMA, measured +7%+7\% at 819238192^{3} and +16%+16\% at 10240310240^{3} over a 16-way unroll.

  • •

    bf16-output store. The fp32 accumulator is down-converted in-register by a 2-wide round-to-nearest-even convertor, then written with a 2-byte block store, which halves the store traffic of the earlier fp32 path and removes the fp32 global round trip. This matches the oneDNN output dtype; the co-measured bf16/fp32 time ratio is 0.95 on a healthy node.

D.2.1. Collaborative de-duplicated inner loop

The partial-tile policy keeps the same demand loads and DPAS contraction but replaces full-tile warming with partial-tile ownership. The 32 subgroups form an 8×48{\times}4 grid. For A, the four subgroup columns partition each 32×3232{\times}32 tile into row slices; for B, the subgroup-row indices partition its K extent and select one 32-column half. These offsets cover the distinct workgroup panel exactly once. Unlike the earlier full-tile cooperative-prefetch experiment, this path has no split barrier.

⬇
// Collaborative partial-tile ownership arithmetic.
const int coop_h_idx = sg_id % (256 / BN);
const int coop_v_idx = sg_id / (256 / BN);
const int pref_a_row_offset = BM / (256 / BN);
const int pref_b_sg_row_size = 256 / (BM * 2);
const int pref_b_row_offset = BK / (256 / BN);
const int coop_b_row_idx = coop_v_idx % pref_b_sg_row_size;
const int coop_b_col_idx = coop_v_idx / pref_b_sg_row_size;
const int coop_a_row_offset = coop_h_idx * pref_a_row_offset;
const int coop_b_row_offset = coop_b_row_idx * pref_b_row_offset;
const int coop_b_col_offset = coop_b_col_idx * 32;
int prefetch_a = GEMM_PF_A;
int prefetch_b = GEMM_PF_B;
// De-duplicated prologue: use the same disjoint slices as steady state.
#pragma unroll
for (int k = 0; k < prefetch_a; k++)
prefetch_load_coop(a_reg, g_a, {0, 0, wg_m, k},
{coop_a_row_offset, 0});
#pragma unroll
for (int k = 0; k < prefetch_b; k++)
prefetch_load_coop(b_reg, g_b, {0, 0, k, wg_n},
{coop_b_row_offset, coop_b_col_offset});
#pragma unroll GEMM_UNROLL
for (int k = 0; k < GK / BK; k++, prefetch_a++, prefetch_b++) {
load(a_reg, g_a, {0, 0, wg_m, k});
load(b_reg, g_b, {0, 0, k, wg_n});
if (prefetch_a < GK / BK)
prefetch_load_coop(a_reg, g_a, {0, 0, wg_m, prefetch_a},
{coop_a_row_offset, 0});
if (prefetch_b < GK / BK)
prefetch_load_coop(b_reg, g_b, {0, 0, prefetch_b, wg_n},
{coop_b_row_offset, coop_b_col_offset});
mma_AB(c_reg, a_reg, b_reg, c_reg);
}

The loop needs no producer-consumer split, SLM staging, multi-stage buffer rotation, or barrier. ThunderKittens instead splits its pipeline across producer and consumer warpgroups and waits on a semaphore at every K step, while the HipKittens loop issues two workgroup barriers per matrix instruction.

Each prefetch_load_coop call lowers its assigned offset to one Intel 2-D block-prefetch instruction with a 16×816{\times}8 element block and count two. Across the workgroup, the calls warm 32,768 bytes per K-step, equal to the distinct A+B footprint, versus approximately 118,784 bytes for the masked full-tile path. The same assignment is used in the prologue; de-duplicated priming adds a 0.8% geometric-mean gain on small and medium squares.

D.3. Methodology

Measurements use the shared single-GPU isolation protocol. oneDNN and SyclKittens are loaded into one process and timed in an interleaved round robin. Each trial uses 10 warmup and 30 measured iterations and rotates the implementation that starts first. Interleaving reduces clock drift in the SyclKittens/oneDNN ratio.

Within a node, each value is the per-shape median of per-trial ratios. The reported ratios are medians of the six node medians. Before a shape enters the results tables, its output is checked against torch.mm by relative Frobenius norm. All measured configurations pass, with maximum error 1.663×10−31.663\times 10^{-3}.

D.4. De-Duplicated-Prefetch Performance

Matched cumulative tail.

The final three cumulative stages share shapes, output type, launch policy, correctness gate, and six-node co-measurement. They isolate snake traversal, partial-tile ownership de-duplication, and shape-specific prefetch distance.

Across all shapes, de-duplication improves the geometric mean by 1.056×1.056\times. Shape-specific prefetch distances produce the final 96.3%96.3\% configuration.

Every value is a six-node cross-node median from co-measured trials using the loop in §D.2.1. Ratios use measured oneDNN throughput as the denominator.

SyclKittens exceeds oneDNN on three of the 27 shapes.

D.5. Correctness

All 27 shapes pass the relative-Frobenius-norm gate ∥C−ref∥F/∥ref∥F<0.02\lVert C-\mathrm{ref}\rVert_{F}/\lVert\mathrm{ref}\rVert_{F}<0.02. Every shape reports a uniform relative error of 1.66×10−31.66\times 10^{-3}, the expected bf16 rounding floor for these accumulation depths, with no per-shape outlier. The bf16-output store retains the fp32 output path’s accuracy.

D.6. Triton-XPU Comparison

One sweep co-measures oneDNN, the final cooperative SyclKittens revision, and Intel Triton-XPU 3.6 over the same 27 BF16 input/output shapes. For each shape on each node, we independently autotune Triton and record its best configuration for comparison. Each trial rotates their execution order, with 10 warmup iterations and 30 timed iterations per implementation; host timing includes an explicit XPU completion barrier. Each implementation is checked against the same fp32 torch.mm reference.

Ratios are reduced first by the median across 10 trials within each node and then by the median across six nodes. The final cooperative SyclKittens reaches 1.087×1.087\times geometric-mean and 1.030×1.030\times median throughput over Triton. The cross-node median exceeds Triton on all 27 shapes; the smallest margin is 1.0125×1.0125\times. Table 24 shows that the advantage holds for both square and rectangular workloads.

Across the six nodes, the 27-shape SyclKittens/Triton geometric mean ranges from 1.084×1.084\times to 1.095×1.095\times, so the advantage does not depend on which node measures it. The maximum SyclKittens and Triton relative Frobenius errors against the reference are both 1.663×10−31.663\times 10^{-3}, so both implementations clear the same accuracy bar.

D.7. Split-K / Stream-K Design

The SyclKittens atomic-combine split-K path targets occupancy-starved decode, QKV-projection, and MoE-expert shapes with small M,NM,N, large KK, and an L2-resident output. Eight compile-time K planes reuse the base mainloop and atomically combine fp32 accumulators before one bf16 output round.

D.7.1. Delivered performance (M=N=512M{=}N{=}512, K sweep)

The oneDNN baseline is torch.mm (bf16 in, bf16 out); “auto” denotes the auto-selected split (S=8S{=}8). All results pass relative-Frobenius <2×10−6<2\times 10^{-6}.

The default kernel remains at 21–24 TFLOPS because 128 workgroups under-fill the machine while the serial mainloop grows with KK. Split-K is 2.4–6.9× faster than that default and exceeds oneDNN by up to 1.21× for K≤16384K\leq 16384. At K=32768K=32768, oneDNN also uses K-parallelism and reaches 169.9 TFLOPS versus 163.7 TFLOPS for split-K.

D.7.2. Correctness

The atomic-add epilogue is bit-exact against the plain-store epilogue in all 10 unit-test cases (relative-Frobenius error zero).

Appendix E Attention Forward (MHA and GQA)

The fence-free adaptive forward-attention kernel reaches 71.7 TFLOPS for MHA and 75.7 TFLOPS for GQA on one GPU. Across non-causal and causal modes, its geometric-mean speedups over IPEX SDPA are 1.091.09–1.21×1.21\times for MHA and 1.701.70–4.0×4.0\times for GQA.

E.1. Configuration

MHA is characterized at B=4B=4 (throughput regime); the GQA performance tables in Sec. E.4 measure batch-one full-sequence queries at B=1B=1. The GQA runtime selection policy is a 2-D function of (N,B)(N,B) (Sec. E.5), retuned across B∈{1,2,4,8}B\in\{1,2,4,8\} for full-sequence attention. GQA is compared against SDPA with IPEX imported and enable_gqa=True. This suite measurement uses its grouped-head fallback, which repeats KV heads, rather than the separately measured pre-expanded-KV fast path. The controlled agent study uses native PyTorch XPU SDPA without importing IPEX. There is no Triton grouped-attention baseline.

E.2. Kernel Implementation and Key Techniques

The MHA implementation is a single-pass, register-resident FlashAttention-style kernel (Dao et al., 2022) built on ThunderKittens tile primitives and specialized for the Intel Max GPU (Xe) DPAS matrix engine. It is templated on head dimension, work-group size, query-tile length, and causality, so one compiled module holds every tuned variant and runtime dispatch selects the measured work-group size and query-tile length (co-loading separately compiled variants is not possible, since their generated kernel symbols collide).

Data flow (per query tile).

Each subgroup owns a seq_q×D\text{seq\_q}\times D query tile and streams the KV sequence in kv_stride=32\text{kv\_stride}=32 chunks. For every KV tile, the kernel computes S=Q​K⊤S=QK^{\top} with mma<N,T>, accumulating inner_loop=D/32=4\text{inner\_loop}=D/32=4 DPAS contractions into an S⁡[seq_q×32]S[\text{seq\_q}\times 32] register tile. It then applies the optional causal mask, updates the online softmax’s running maximum and normalizer, rescales the output accumulator, and accumulates O+=P​VO\mathrel{+}=PV with mma<N,N>. After the KV loop, OO is normalized by the running sum and stored.

Key techniques.
  • •

    Online softmax and scaling. The N×NN\times N score matrix is never materialized. The running max (max_vec), normalizer (norm_vec), and output accumulator remain in registers, with the accumulator rescaled by e(mold−mnew)e^{(m_{\text{old}}-m_{\text{new}})} at each KV step. Folding 1/D1/\sqrt{D} with log2⁡e=1.44269504\log_{2}e=1.44269504 maps p=exp2​(S⋅scale−m)p=\text{exp2}(S\cdot\text{scale}-m) directly to the hardware exp2 unit.

  • •

    Register reuse and pipelining. The seq_q×D\text{seq\_q}\times D query tile is loaded once before the KV loop, avoiding a reload for every KV tile. Software prefetch issues the next K/V loads while DPAS consumes the current tile. Hardware dependency tokens order load-to-DPAS and DPAS-to-consumer hazards without software scoreboard drains; a 4-seed ×\times 20-repeat ablation measured up to a ∼\sim15% cost from those drains at large-NN causal, with no correctness benefit.

  • •

    DPAS accumulator and operand layouts. For D>64D>64, split-D accumulation carries the output in two D/2D/2-wide accumulators with independent V loads and DPAS, preserving the 32×3232\times 32 DPAS shape and register budget. The block loads map row-major A, transposed B for mma<N,T>, and VNNI-packed column-major B for mma<N,N>; a mismatched role corrupts SS or OO. The transposed-B load lets the matrix engine consume K⊤K^{\top} directly without explicit lane-shuffle repacking.

  • •

    Query tiling and causal scheduling. Setting seq_q=8\text{seq\_q}=8 halves rows per subgroup and doubles concurrent query tiles; it is selected at small NN, with the crossover to seq_q=16\text{seq\_q}=16 determined by the MHA or GQA dispatch table below. The causal loop omits fully masked upper-triangle KV tiles and masks only the diagonal tile across kv_stride/seq_q\text{kv\_stride}/\text{seq\_q} sub-blocks, namely two for seq_q=16\text{seq\_q}=16 and four for seq_q=8\text{seq\_q}=8. Reverse linear query ordering dispatches the heaviest causal blocks first to balance workgroups.

  • •

    Head mapping and grid residency. Query head hh maps to KV head ⌊h/(H/Hk​v)⌋\lfloor h/(H/H_{kv})\rfloor; MHA is the group-size-one specialization, with separate tuned dispatch parameters (Sec. E.5). Avoiding forced root synchronization lets the full grid run concurrently instead of limiting residency to approximately one workgroup per compute core, improving large-NN throughput by up to ∼\sim16×\times.

  • •

    Split-K forward. When KV depth per GPU leaves execution resources idle, workers process separate KV partitions and write partial OO/max/norm states. A small log-sum-exp kernel merges them, improving performance by 0.6–2.9% at N≥4096N\geq 4096.

E.3. Methodology

Each (N,config)(N,\text{config}) runs in a separate subprocess pinned to one GPU, with at most one heavy task per GPU. Baseline, SyclKittens, and Triton are interleaved within each trial; GQA compares only the baseline and SyclKittens. Each of 10 independent trials uses 10 warmup and 30 measured iterations. TFLOPS is the trial mean, with standard deviation shown where applicable; GQA values are additionally averaged over three independent runs.

Non-causal forward attention counts 4​B​H​N2​D4\,BHN^{2}D FLOPs. The causal count uses the same coefficient over lower-triangular work, so each path is directly comparable with its own baseline. Every configuration is checked against a PyTorch reference before inclusion (Sec. E.6).

E.4. Delivered Performance

Numbers use the validated adaptive runtime policy rather than separately compiled per-shape kernels.

E.4.1. MHA (adaptive kernel, B=4B=4, H=16H=16, D=128D=128)

The model output contract and SDPA baseline require bf16 output, so the reported measurements include the fp32-to-bf16 epilogue conversion. At 50% occupancy, this conversion spills the seq_q=16\text{seq\_q}=16 epilogue; omitting it and returning fp32 is 12% faster at small NN and 4% at large NN. Store-payload reshaping and a compiler register-pressure cap both increased runtime.

At N=512N=512, the selected causal variant reaches 1.42×1.42\times IPEX and 1.87×1.87\times Triton. Its seq_q=8\text{seq\_q}=8 tile doubles concurrent query tiles, skips fully masked upper-triangle KV blocks, and applies masking only to the diagonal block, reducing executed Q​K⊤QK^{\top}, softmax, and P​VPV work.

E.4.2. GQA (adaptive kernel, B=1B=1, H=32H=32, Hk​v=8H_{kv}=8, D=128D=128)

The tables below characterize full-sequence GQA at B=1B=1, compared against SDPA with grouped-query attention enabled; numbers are the mean of three independent single-GPU runs. The runtime selection policy also covers B∈{2,4,8}B\in\{2,4,8\} (Sec. E.5), where the selected variant differs from B=1B=1.

The causal separation follows from the baseline’s loss of parallelism at the single-batch grouped shape beyond N=4096N=4096. The adaptive GQA kernel retains parallelism, and its N≤1024N\leq 1024 causal configurations select seq_q=8\text{seq\_q}=8 (Sec. E.5).

E.5. Autotune Grid and Selection Policy

The grid sweep covers workgroup size ∈{64,128,256}×seq_q∈{8,16}\in\{64,128,256\}\times\text{seq\_q}\in\{8,16\}, swept over all NN for both masks.

The dispatch function encodes this table in a compile-time MHA branch, independent of the GQA policy. Handling the narrow seq_q=8\text{seq\_q}=8 register tile in the causal masking routine makes this configuration available and yields the 1.42×1.42\times result at N=512N=512.

GQA 2-D (N,B)(N,B) policy (compile-time else branch, group size 4).

Unlike MHA, the selected GQA configuration depends on both sequence length NN and batch BB. At low grid occupancy, seq_q=8\text{seq\_q}=8 doubles the number of concurrent query tiles. As BB fills the machine, the selected seq_q=16\text{seq\_q}=16 crossover moves to smaller NN, and larger workgroups are selected more often.

The batch-aware sweep spans B∈{1,2,4,8}B\in\{1,2,4,8\}, N∈{256,512,1024,2048}N\in\{256,512,1024,2048\}, workgroup size ∈{64,128,256}\in\{64,128,256\}, and seq_q∈{8,16}\text{seq\_q}\in\{8,16\} at decoder-model dimensions. Each cell has 24 repetitions and must pass a ≥200\geq 200 TFLOPS calibration gate with coefficient of variation ≤7%\leq 7\%. The tables report the selected workgroup size and seq_q with median latency in parentheses.

Indexing the policy only by the B=1B=1 measurements selects the wrong configuration after the crossover at B≥2B\geq 2. For causal N=1024N=1024, applying the B=1B=1 selection (128 work-items and eight query rows) at B=4B=4 takes 681 µs, 20% longer than 128 work-items and 16 query rows at 569 µs; at B=8B=8, the difference is 38%. The 2-D dispatch function encodes these selections using pre-instantiated variants. Workgroup size depends on both batch and sequence length, even for a fixed query-tile size. The B=1B=1 selections and the N>2048N>2048 long-context selection (256 work-items and 16 query rows) are preserved.
