Appendix F Memory-Bound Norms, RoPE, and Decode GEMV

Root mean square layer normalization (RMSNorm) (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019), layer normalization (LayerNorm) (Ba et al., 2016), rotary position embedding (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), and single-token GEMV all depend on wide coalesced memory access, with subgroup cooperation added where a row reduction is required. Norms and RoPE are compared with eager PyTorch and torch.compile (TorchInductor to Triton on Intel Max GPU); decode GEMV is compared with the tuned vendor library path (oneMKL).

F.1. Configuration

RMSNorm uses D=2048D=2048 and LayerNorm D=4096D=4096, with bf16 inputs/outputs, fp32 accumulation, and ϵ=10−5\epsilon=10^{-5}. We test (B,N)∈{(1,1),(1,64),(1,512),(4,1024),(16,2048),(64,2048)}(B,N)\in\{(1,1),(1,64),(1,512),(4,1024),(16,2048),(64,2048)\} on one GPU. Plain norms read and write 2​B​N​D2BND elements; fused residual-add, norm, and residual writeback read and write 4​B​N​D4BND elements. The measured kernels assign eight cooperating subgroups to each row and use 128-bit load_wide/store_wide transactions.

Reported useful traffic is 2​B​N​D⋅22\,BND\cdot 2 bytes for plain norm and 4​B​N​D⋅24\,BND\cdot 2 bytes for fused norm at 2 B/elem. This common accounting convention makes the GB/s columns comparable; it excludes extra intermediate traffic in implementations that launch multiple kernels.

F.2. Kernel Implementation and Key Techniques

Each norm is a single translation unit templated on row width, subgroups per row, and whether to add and write back the residual. It is built into a per-width pybind11 module with separate plain and fused entry points. The kernel is written entirely in SyclKittens, with no hand-rolled intrinsics, on top of the load_wide/store_wide 128-bit vector-memory ops.

Data flow (per row). The grid is (1,B,N)(1,B,N) with WPR⋅16\mathrm{WPR}\cdot 16 threads per block. One work-group owns each row, and its WPR\mathrm{WPR} subgroups cooperate. Subgroup ww owns the contiguous slice x[row,w⋅DC:(w+1)⋅DC]x[\mathrm{row},w{\cdot}DC:(w{+}1){\cdot}DC] in an rv_fl<DC, naive> register vector. This uses D​C/16DC/16 fp32 values per lane, 16 at D=2048D=2048 and 32 at D=4096D=4096, both within the register file.

Each subgroup loads its chunk with load_wide. In the fused path it adds the residual chunk and writes the residual sum with store_wide. The subgroup then computes its partial moment or moments and publishes them to SLM. After one group_barrier, every subgroup reads all partials, forms the row statistic, applies the affine transform, and writes its output chunk with store_wide.

Key techniques.

  • •

    Cooperative multi-subgroup row decomposition. Splitting the row across WPR=8\mathrm{WPR}=8 subgroups reduces per-lane accumulators from D/16D/16 (single-subgroup layout with 128 at D=2048D{=}2048, 256 at D=4096D{=}4096, which spills) to D/(16​WPR)D/(16\,\mathrm{WPR}) (16 / 32, no spill). This decomposition increases measured LayerNorm bandwidth from ∼\sim570 to ∼\sim970–1100 GB/s.

  • •

    128-bit coalesced load_wide/store_wide. Each lane issues a full uint4 (16 B) per transaction; 16 lanes touch 256 contiguous bytes in one cache-line-aligned burst (interleaved-128 mapping), the widest transaction the Intel Max GPU memory pipe accepts. The old scalar rv_fl fallback issued 32-bit strided loads at ≤\leqhalf the effective bandwidth. Requires D​CDC a multiple of 128 and a 16 B-aligned base (satisfied for D∈{1024,2048,4096}D\in\{1024,2048,4096\}).

  • •

    SLM moment reduction. RMSNorm reduces one moment (∑x2\sum x^{2}) through a WPR\mathrm{WPR}-float SLM scratch; LayerNorm reduces two (∑x\sum x, ∑x2\sum x^{2}) through 2⋅WPR2\cdot\mathrm{WPR} floats, then forms μ=1D​∑x\mu=\tfrac{1}{D}\sum x, σ2=1D​∑x2−μ2\sigma^{2}=\tfrac{1}{D}\sum x^{2}-\mu^{2}. A single group_barrier separates publish from read-back.

  • •

    Single-launch fused residual path. The kernel folds the x+residualx+\mathrm{residual} add into the load and emits the residual sum, so the pre-norm transformer’s reused hidden state h=x+sub⁡(x)h=x+\mathrm{sub}(x) is materialized without a second kernel or a re-read of hh.

  • •

    Register-fused affine + rsqrt. inv​_​std=rsqrt⁡(var+eps)\mathrm{inv\_std}=\mathrm{rsqrt}(\mathrm{var}+\mathrm{eps}) maps to the hardware reciprocal-sqrt unit; the normalize, scale (γ\gamma), and shift (β\beta, LayerNorm) are fused in registers before the store, with γ\gamma/β\beta themselves streamed via load_wide.

F.3. Methodology

Measurements follow the shared isolation protocol on one selected GPU. Eager F.rms_norm/F.layer_norm decomposes RMSNorm into multiple kernels; torch.compile lowers the same operations through Inductor to Triton on XPU.

For the fused comparison, SyclKittens writes both the normalized output and residual sum (4×4\times traffic). The expression torch.compile(F.rms_norm(x+res)) discards the sum (3×3\times) and is approximately 30% faster at identical bandwidth. All three measured implementations therefore return (norm, x+res) and use the same useful-byte denominator. An unfused add-then-norm that retains the residual moves 5×5\times traffic; the fused both-output kernel moves 4×4\times, a 20% traffic reduction.

The three implementations are interleaved round-robin within each of 10 trials, each with 10 warmup and 30 measured iterations; tables report the per-configuration median. A 2 s GEMM power-condition burn-in precedes measurement, and the Inductor graph-cache limit is 64 to prevent eager fallback. All cold-HBM tables use one cache protocol, in which a ∼\sim256 MB buffer is zeroed before every timed call to evict L2, following Triton’s convention, so all reads miss to HBM. Without eviction, small-BB working sets below the ∼\sim204 MB per-GPU L2 report cache bandwidth above the HBM roofline. Warm steady-state latency is recorded separately for decode.

Traffic is 2​B​N​D⋅22\,BND\cdot 2 B for plain norm and 4​B​N​D⋅24\,BND\cdot 2 B for fused norm; GB/s is traffic divided by median time. Before timing, each configuration checks the plain norm, fused norm, and residual store against a PyTorch reference with relative error below 2​e−22\mathrm{e}{-2}.

F.4. Delivered Performance

The norm tables below report per-configuration cold-HBM medians. SyclKittens/eager is the speedup over eager PyTorch, and SyclKittens/compile is the speedup over torch.compile.

F.4.1. RMSNorm (D=2048D=2048)

Plain, geomean 1.12×\times over torch.compile, 15.6×\times over eager.

Fused (residual + norm, 4×4\times), geomean 1.04×\times over torch.compile.

F.4.2. LayerNorm (D=4096D=4096)

Plain, geomean 1.42×\times over torch.compile, 2.78×\times over eager.

Fused (residual + norm, 4×4\times), geomean 1.12×\times over torch.compile.

For the HBM-bound shapes (B≥16B\geq 16), eager PyTorch sustains ∼\sim45–320 GB/s because its decomposition traverses the data in several kernels. Triton fusion raises torch.compile to 517–877 GB/s on LayerNorm, while SyclKittens sustains 623–997 GB/s (1.08–1.63×\times). At the two large RMSNorm cells, both paths approach the ∼\sim1.3 TB/s per-GPU roofline and differ by 0.99–1.05×\times; at B=4B=4, lower launch overhead gives SyclKittens a 1.13–1.33×\times advantage.

F.5. Decode/Dispatch-Bound Latency

For few-token decode shapes, each norm touches at most 512 rows and fixed launch overhead dominates. SyclKittens uses one Level-Zero submission; torch.compile incurs a Dynamo guard and Triton launch, while eager uses multiple kernels. The preceding matmul or attention leaves the decode norm input L2-resident, so the table reports warm steady-state latency for that cache state.

For fused residual-add and norm, SyclKittens holds a warm median ∼\sim24 µs dispatch floor across the sweep while torch.compile sits at ∼\sim55–61 µs.

SyclKittens’s near-flat latency (24.2–24.6 µs for RMSNorm and 23.6–23.7 µs for LayerNorm) reflects one fused submission. The torch.compile floor is ∼\sim2.3–2.6×\times higher, while eager latency grows with NN as its decomposed operations re-traverse each row.

F.6. Correctness

Every configuration is validated before timing, namely the plain norm and fused norm against a PyTorch fp32-reference (relative error), and the residual sum x+resx+\mathrm{res} byte-exactly. Representative maxima appear below.

All configurations pass; the residual store is exact (both SyclKittens and Inductor write the same x+resx+\mathrm{res}). The larger RMSNorm rel-err (2.8e-3 versus 1.4e-5 for LayerNorm) reflects bf16 rounding of the un-centered second moment.

F.7. Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) with 128-bit Chunk-Pair Mapping

RoPE is the transformer block’s other memory-bound elementwise op. The 128-bit coalesced kernel reaches 1020 GB/s. Relative to torch.compile, its geometric-mean speedups are 1.09×1.09\times for cold bandwidth-bound shapes and 1.98×1.98\times for warm decode shapes.

F.7.1. Configuration

We evaluate halved rotary with D=128D=128, H=32H=32, bf16 inputs/outputs, and fp32 computation on the same six (B,N)(B,N) cells as the norms. Baselines are eager PyTorch and torch.compile; useful traffic is 2​B​N​H​D⋅22BNHD\cdot 2 bytes for one input read and output write.

F.7.2. Wide Chunk-Pair Mapping

RoPE couples element dd with d+64d+64 across the two halves of a head. A contiguous wide load groups eight adjacent bf16 elements, so it never places a rotary pair on the same lane. The SyclKittens load_wide also requires a 128-element multiple and is designed for reductions, so it cannot be used unchanged. The kernel instead re-tiles the raw 128-bit packing from the earlier hand-tuned norm kernel for rotary pairs.

  • •

    One work-item owns one 8-element chunk-pair. Work-item (row,c)(\mathrm{row},c) takes the cc-th 8-wide chunk of the first half, x1[c⋅8:c⋅8+8]x_{1}[c{\cdot}8:c{\cdot}8{+}8], and its partner chunk in the second half, x2[c⋅8:c⋅8+8]x_{2}[c{\cdot}8:c{\cdot}8{+}8], 64 bf16 elements away. Since D=128D=128, there are 8 chunk-pairs per head; consecutive work-items read consecutive 16-byte words, so each subgroup’s transaction is a fully coalesced 256-byte burst.

  • •

    Four 16-byte loads, two 16-byte stores, all coalesced. Each item issues one uint4 load apiece for its x1x_{1}, x2x_{2}, cos, and sin chunks. Each load is 16 B, or eight bf16 elements. The item computes the eight rotary pairs in fp32 registers and stores the two output chunks as two uint4 writes. Every xx/out transaction is the widest the Intel Max GPU pipe accepts.

  • •

    Local pair computation. RoPE requires no SLM, barrier, or shuffle because each chunk-pair is local to one work-item. This mapping exposes independent work at high occupancy. It requires DD to be a multiple of 16 and the base to be 16 B aligned, as it is for contiguous [B,N,H,D][B,N,H,D] bf16 with D=128D=128.

F.7.3. Delivered Performance

RoPE follows the shared interleaved-trial and power-conditioning methodology. The bandwidth table uses the cold-HBM protocol; the decode table uses warm, L2-resident inputs. SyclKittens/eager is the speedup over eager, and SyclKittens/compile is the speedup over torch.compile.

Bandwidth (HBM-bound, L2 flushed before every call, cold), geomean 1.09×\times over torch.compile.

At B=64B{=}64, SyclKittens measures 1020 GB/s and torch.compile measures 882 GB/s; the large-BB norm kernels measure 980–997 GB/s.

Decode/dispatch-bound (warm, L2-resident input), latency (µs), geomean 1.98×\times over torch.compile.

As with the norms, SyclKittens holds a near-flat ∼\sim27–31 µs single-launch floor across the few-token sweep while torch.compile sits ∼\sim1.9–2.1×\times higher. The difference is one Level-Zero submission versus a Dynamo guard followed by a Triton launch.

F.7.4. Correctness

Every config is validated before timing against an fp32 reference (relative-error tolerance 2e-2). SyclKittens computes the halved rotary in fp32 and rounds to bf16 identically to the reference, making the result bit-exact. The measured relative error is 0.00.0 at all six shapes, matching torch.compile.

F.8. Single-Token Decode GEMV (M=1M=1)

The decode-time weight projections (Wq​k​vW_{qkv}, WoW_{o}, Wg​a​t​eW_{gate}, Wu​pW_{up}, Wd​o​w​nW_{down}) are matrix-vector products out⁡[N]=W⁡[N,K]​@​x​[K]\mathrm{out}[N]=W[N,K]@x[K]. They process one token, so M=1M=1. Their arithmetic intensity is approximately one FLOP per byte of streamed weights. The kernel streams all of WW (N⋅K⋅2N{\cdot}K{\cdot}2 B) once and does ∼\sim2 FLOP/element. These five projections account for approximately 64%64\% of per-token decode latency, and their throughput is determined by bf16 weight-streaming bandwidth.

The DPAS systolic array requires M≥8M\geq 8, so M=1M=1 uses at most one eighth of that matrix shape. For this GEMV comparison, we call oneMKL oneapi::mkl::blas::gemm directly. Eager F.linear and torch.compile instead reach the corresponding oneDNN GEMM path through PyTorch; on this platform the two entry points share the underlying GEMM implementation.

F.8.1. Configuration

We evaluate the five Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori and others, 2024) M=1M=1 projections at TP=1=1, namely Wq​k​vW_{qkv} (6144×40966144\times 4096), WoW_{o} (4096×40964096\times 4096), Wg​a​t​eW_{gate} and Wu​pW_{up} (14336×409614336\times 4096), and Wd​o​w​nW_{down} (4096×143364096\times 14336). Inputs and outputs are bf16 with fp32 accumulation. The tuned vendor library path is oneMKL GEMM plus its fp32-to-bf16 cast; SyclKittens uses eight split-K subgroups per output row, 256-element software-prefetched chunks, and a direct bf16 store.

F.8.2. Split-K Streaming Reduction

A GEMV row is a dot product, structurally the RMSNorm per-row reduction with the weight row in place of xx. The kernel reuses the same SyclKittens wide-load reduction, restructured for the M=1M=1 occupancy problem.

  • •

    Split-K occupancy. One workgroup owns each output row and WPR\mathrm{WPR} subgroups divide its KK reduction. The norms use the same decomposition to fit registers; here it also increases parallel work. Total launched work is N⋅WPR⋅16N{\cdot}\mathrm{WPR}{\cdot}16 threads, so it still scales with NN, but each row supplies multiple cooperating subgroups. This reduces sensitivity to the output-row count relative to oneMKL, as the tensor-parallel sweep below shows.

  • •

    128-bit coalesced load_wide over the KK-slice. Each subgroup streams its contiguous slice W[n,w⋅DC:(w+1)⋅DC]W[n,w{\cdot}DC:(w{+}1){\cdot}DC] (D​C=K/WPRDC=K/\mathrm{WPR}) in CHUNK\mathrm{CHUNK}-wide pieces via the same load_wide (uint4/lane, 256 B/subgroup-transaction) that took the norms to line rate. A narrow 16-bit, one-workgroup-per-row implementation reaches approximately 35% of that rate.

  • •

    Software-prefetched chunks, fp32 accumulate. Chunk c+1c{+}1’s load_wide is issued before the fp32 FMA of chunk cc consumes chunk cc, following the GEMM pipeline in Appendix D. xx is reused across all rows and stays L2-resident.

  • •

    Direct bf16 output. A single-round subgroup sum plus a tiny WPR\mathrm{WPR}-float SLM combine (one group_barrier) yields out⁡[n]\mathrm{out}[n], written straight to bf16. The oneMKL path uses an fp32 scratch buffer and a separate cast kernel, adding one launch and N⋅(4+2)N{\cdot}(4{+}2) B of traffic.

WPR=8,CHUNK=256\mathrm{WPR}=8,\mathrm{CHUNK}=256 requires Kmod2048=0K\bmod 2048=0 (holds for all five unsharded shapes); TP-sharded variants must also satisfy this constraint, and other KK fall back to oneMKL. The kernel is written on the SyclKittens load_wide/rv_fl/sum operations, no hand-rolled intrinsics. A hardware L1-prefetch variant of load_wide also exists in SyclKittens but is not used here. With only 2–7 chunks per slice, the register double-buffer already covers the latency; measurements showed no benefit and occasional regression from the extra prefetch.

F.8.3. Delivered Performance

Each shape reports the median (p50) over 300 individually event-timed iterations; the harness also records p95/p99. The table uses the shared cold-HBM cache protocol, so WW is read from HBM on every call. SyclKittens/oneMKL is the speedup over the oneMKL decode path; %roof uses the measured ∼\sim1.3 TB/s per-GPU streaming-HBM reference. The specification is 1.6 TB/s, and the large-operand kernels above approach a ∼\sim990 GB/s asymptote.

Cold HBM, geomean 1.36×\times over oneMKL.

Summed per-token GEMM latency (5 GEMVs ×\times 32 layers, TP=1=1) falls from oneMKL 36.3 ms to SyclKittens 27.2 ms (1.33×\times). A naive one-work-group-per-row bf16 stream (narrow 16-bit loads plus a 256-wide reduce) is slower than oneMKL (42.2 ms, 0.86×0.86\times), establishing that the wide-load and split-K structure produces the measured improvement.

The kernel is latency-stable, because cold p99 is within ≤\leq5% of p50 on every shape, so the p99 per-token GEMM is 28.4 ms (SyclKittens) vs 38.1 ms (oneMKL), the 1.33×1.33\times holds at the tail. The L2-resident regime (per-op timed) gives 14.7 ms to 10.7 ms per token, 1.37×1.37\times.

Cold and L2-resident regimes. A single cold GEMV reads 33–117 MB from an idle memory pipeline and sustains 490–531 GB/s; the 0.5–1 GB norm streams approach the 990 GB/s long-stream asymptote. With weights resident in the 204 MB L2 and no flush, SyclKittens reaches 1060–1380 GB/s, 82–106% of the 1.3 TB/s HBM reference, and 10.7 ms/token. Values above 100% reflect L2 bandwidth.

The approximately 16-GB model weights do not fit in L2, while the 160 GEMVs per token execute consecutively, placing decode between these two measurements. Across both regimes, SyclKittens exceeds oneMKL, with ratios of 1.24–1.53×\times cold and 1.02–1.90×\times resident, with an approximately 1.36×\times geometric mean in each. Split-K occupancy and removal of the cast and scratch path apply in both cache states.

F.8.4. TP Sharding and Output-Dimension Occupancy

Inference runs tensor-parallel, so the column-parallel projections (Wq​k​vW_{qkv}, Wg​a​t​eW_{gate}, Wu​pW_{up}) shard the output dimension NN to N/nN/n at TP=n=n. We emulate TP=n=n by running the per-shard (N/n,K)(N/n,K) GEMV on a single GPU with the same algorithm. The SyclKittens/oneMKL cold-HBM ratio rises monotonically with nn. Values are per-shape cold p50, reproducible across two runs, with fixed WPR=8\mathrm{WPR}=8.

oneMKL’s M=1M{=}1 GEMM parallelism is its output-tile count ⌈N/BN⌉\lceil N/B_{N}\rceil, so as NN shrinks it loses tiles and its bandwidth falls from 360 to 135 GB/s for Wq​k​vW_{qkv} as NN goes from 6144 to 768. SyclKittens’s split-K makes launched work N⋅WPRN\cdot\mathrm{WPR} (still ≥6144\geq 6144 subgroups at N=768N=768), so it declines only gently (503 to 323). The ratio widens because oneMKL loses output-tile parallelism faster; both paths slow at smaller NN. Ratios separate this occupancy effect from the latency reduction caused by smaller shards.

Row-parallel WoW_{o}/Wd​o​w​nW_{down} instead shard KK with NN fixed at 4096. Their parallelism and ratio remain unchanged, isolating output-dimension occupancy as the cause of the widening column-parallel ratio. The ratio reaches 2.4×\times at TP=8=8. A fixed WPR=8\mathrm{WPR}=8 captures this effect; a per-shape WPR⁡(N)\mathrm{WPR}(N) sweep found no further gain, since even the smallest shard already saturates at WPR=8\mathrm{WPR}=8 and larger WPR\mathrm{WPR} only adds combine overhead.

F.8.5. Correctness

Each shape is checked against an fp32 reference out_ref=(W.float()@x.float())\mathrm{out\_ref}=(W.\mathrm{float}()@x.\mathrm{float}()) before timing. SyclKittens accumulates in fp32 and applies one bf16 round on store, so its max-abs error is identical to the oneMKL path (both round an O⁡(K)O(\sqrt{K})-magnitude sum once). The error is in {0.50,0.50,0.80,0.50,0.99}\{0.50,0.50,0.80,0.50,0.99\} for the five shapes, reflecting bf16 output quantization. All shapes match oneMKL to the last bf16 ULP band.

Appendix G Op-Fusion Microbenchmarks

Fusing Q/K rotary combines two launches and allows cached cos/sin data to be reused across both tensors. We compare this path with eager PyTorch and torch.compile (TorchInductor to Triton on Intel Max GPU) using the cold/warm methodology from Appendix F; Section K.4 measures the complete composed path.

G.1. Fused Q/K Rotary

Every decoder layer, before attention, applies RoPE to both the projected query and key. For Mistral-7B (Jiang et al., 2023) and Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori and others, 2024) GQA, H=32H=32 query heads, Hk​v=8H_{kv}=8 key heads, and D=128D=128. The baseline launches Q and K rotary separately over the shared (N,D/2)(N,D/2) tables. The fused kernel assigns either a Q or K head-row to each work-item and uses identical halved-rotary math.

Traffic ledger.

Both implementations read Q, write Q′Q^{\prime}, read K, and write K′K^{\prime} exactly once. Launch overhead controls few-token decode; fusion reduces two launches to one. The shared (N,D/2)(N,D/2) cos/sin tables are loaded by both Q and K work-items and can be reused through the cache within the same launch. Useful traffic excludes these shared table reads and counts the Q/K tensors. It is therefore 2​B​N​(H+Hk​v)​D⋅22\,B\,N(H+H_{kv})D\cdot 2 bytes (read and write Q and K); at B=64,N=2048B{=}64,N{=}2048 that is 2.68 GB moved in a single launch at 973 GB/s.

G.1.1. Configuration

G.1.2. Kernel implementation and key techniques

The kernel reuses the 128-bit coalesced chunk-pair rotary worker from Appendix F and fuses Q and K by laying their work items end to end in one nd_range, so the linear-id space is the concatenation of Q’s B​N​H⋅CHUNKSB\,N\,H\cdot\text{CHUNKS} items and K’s B​N​Hk​v⋅CHUNKSB\,N\,H_{kv}\cdot\text{CHUNKS} items. A single tid < q_threads test routes each work-item to its tensor with the correct head count; both branches call the same per-row worker. One work-item owns one 8-element chunk-pair of one head-row; with D=128D=128, (D/2)/8=8(D/2)/8=8 chunk-pairs per row. RoPE couples element dd with d+64d{+}64, so each item loads its first-half chunk x1 and its second-half partner x2 (64 bf16 apart) plus the shared cos and sin chunks. That is four coalesced 16-byte loads, the rotary math in fp32 registers, then two 16-byte stores.

⬇
// ONE nd_range whose linear-id space concatenates the Q and K work items:
// q_threads = B*N*H*CHUNKS come first, then k_threads = B*N*HKV*CHUNKS.
// CHUNKS = (D/2)/8 chunk-pairs per row (8 at D=128).
// grid dispatch: one branch selects the sub-grid, both call one worker
const long tid = item.get_global_linear_id();
if (tid < q_threads) // Q sub-grid: heads = H
rotary_row_chunk<D>(q, q_out, cos, sin, /*heads=*/H, N, tid);
else // K sub-grid: heads = HKV
rotary_row_chunk<D>(k, k_out, cos, sin, /*heads=*/HKV, N, tid - q_threads);
// the shared per-row worker (identical math to the unfused rotary)
const long row = local_tid / CHUNKS;
const int chunk = local_tid % CHUNKS;
const int coff = chunk * 8; // bf16 offset within a half
const long row_off = row * D; // (.,N,heads,D) row base
const int n = (row / heads) % N; // seq index for cos/sin
const long cs = n * (D / 2) + coff; // shared cos/sin base
const wide8_t ra = xw[(row_off + coff) / 8];
const wide8_t rb = xw[(row_off + D / 2 + coff) / 8];
const wide8_t rc = cw[cs / 8], rs = sw[cs / 8];
float a[8], b[8], c[8], s[8];
unpack8(ra, a); unpack8(rb, b); unpack8(rc, c); unpack8(rs, s);
float o1[8], o2[8];
#pragma unroll
for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {
o1[i] = a[i] * c[i] - b[i] * s[i]; // rotate first half
o2[i] = b[i] * c[i] + a[i] * s[i]; // rotate second half
}
ow[(row_off + coff) / 8] = pack8(o1); // two coalesced stores
ow[(row_off + D / 2 + coff) / 8] = pack8(o2);

The concatenated id space reduces two Level-Zero submissions to one and permits cached reuse of the shared cos/sin data across Q and K rows. Each work-item uses 128-bit coalesced transactions, the widest accepted by the Intel Max GPU memory path, and requires no SLM, barrier, or shuffle because one work-item owns each rotary pair. Both paths call the same fp32 rotary_row_chunk worker.

G.1.3. Methodology

One heavy task per GPU package, with one stack active, so there is no intra-package HBM contention. The baselines are eager PyTorch and torch.compile(backend="inductor") applied to the same function. Interleaved round-robin timing within each trial keeps implementations under the same clock conditions, controlling drift in the SyclKittens/eager and SyclKittens/compile ratios. Each of 10 trials uses 10 warmup and 30 measured iterations. Each config is measured twice, once warm (operands stay L2-resident, the decode metric) and once cold (a scratch buffer is zeroed to flush L2 before every timed call, following Triton’s cold-cache convention). The cold panel reports HBM bandwidth for the bandwidth-bound shapes; the warm panel reports few-token decode latency. Before timing, rotated Q and K from both SyclKittens and torch.compile are checked against an fp32 reference with relative-error tolerance 2e-2.

G.1.4. Delivered performance

Per-config medians come from 10 co-measured trials of eager PyTorch, torch.compile, and SyclKittens. Bandwidth-bound shapes are reported as cold, L2-flushed HBM bandwidth; the few-token decode shapes as warm dispatch latency. SyclKittens/eager is the speedup over eager, and SyclKittens/compile is the speedup over torch.compile.

Relative to torch.compile, fused Q/K rotary is 1.26–1.69×\times faster for the cold bandwidth-bound shapes and 1.98–2.13×\times faster for the warm decode shapes, where its latency remains 138–149 µs. The gain comes from one joint Q/K launch and reuse of the shared cosine/sine data; torch.compile emits separate guarded rotary launches, while eager decomposes each rotary into several elementwise kernels.

G.1.5. Correctness

Against the fp32 reference rounded to bf16, fused SyclKittens is bit-exact (relative error 0.00.0) at all six benchmark shapes, while torch.compile matches within tolerance. Its maximum absolute difference is 0.0 from both the two-launch unfused rotary path and transformers.apply_rotary_pos_emb, with standalone coverage over B∈{1,2,4,8}×N∈{256,512,1024,2048}B\in\{1,2,4,8\}\times N\in\{256,512,1024,2048\}.

Appendix H Distributed GEMM

The operation starts with row-sharded AA and replicated BB and must return the full replicated C=A​BC=AB on every GPU. Within the original hand-designed input-gather family, the topology-aware path combines an all-gather of AA with the SyclKittens collaborative de-duplicated-prefetch GEMM core. Each source stripe crosses XeLink once per remote GPU package, is replicated to the partner stack over MDFI, and is then consumed by one local GEMM. On 12 GPUs, this path reaches 84% and 93% of its co-measured GEMM-only baseline at 614436144^{3} and 12288312288^{3}. The controlled agent study also explores computing local CC shards first and gathering the output.

H.1. Configuration

A node contains six GPU packages, each with two stacks connected by MDFI, the load/store stack-to-stack interconnect. XeLink connects the GPU packages all-to-all through two independent stack planes, even and odd.

TFLOP/s uses the semantic operation count 2​M​N​K/t2MNK/t per GPU because every GPU returns the full replicated CC. Input-gather methods physically recompute those FLOPs on every GPU; the local-CC family computes one row band per GPU and gathers the completed bands.

H.2. Kernel Implementation and Key Techniques

For the original hand-designed family, the GEMM kernel is DPAS-bound and reaches approximately 90% of its local roofline. Its distributed overhead therefore comes from moving sharded AA across the fabric. These methods use the same compute kernel and differ in how and when they place AA in local HBM.

Input-gather data flow (per GPU).

(1) each GPU owns one M/12×KM/12{\times}K row-shard of AA in local HBM; (2) the missing 11 shards are gathered from peers into a contiguous M×KM{\times}K landing buffer; (3) one register-resident GEMM computes the full C=Afull​BC=A_{\text{full}}B over all MM rows. The methods trade off how step (2) overlaps step (3).

Key techniques
  • •

    Topology-aware gather. Cross XeLink once per stripe and replicate within each GPU package. The 12 stacks are organized as six GPU packages with two stacks each; each pair shares a fast intra-package MDFI link outside the XeLink fabric. Flat all-gather has every stack pull all 11 remote shards, roughly 10 fabric crossings per stack. The topology-aware path sends each source stripe across XeLink exactly once to one landing stack per remote GPU package (landing = 2*q + (p&1)), then the landing stack replicates the shard to its partner (partner(t) = tˆ1) over MDFI. This halves XeLink egress on the communication-bound workload, giving 1.42× (12288312288^{3}) to 2.15× (614436144^{3}) end-to-end distributed-GEMM speedup over the flat gather pipeline in the main paper’s fixed-core movement ablation.

  • •

    Within input-gather schedules, materialize-then-GEMM. The topology-aware path gathers all shards to local HBM and then runs one GEMM. Interleaving the gather into the GEMM mainloop or reading remote AA per DPAS inside the kernel is slower in the measured implementations. Remote operand reads stall the DPAS pipeline, while materialization lets the compute kernel use its local operand-delivery path.

  • •

    Gather topology. DMA memcpy gather and EU vec128 copy gather land within 1% of each other at both shapes; both are fabric-bound. The topology-aware path changes the traffic topology.

  • •

    Large shapes hide communication. At 12288312288^{3} the GEMM is big enough that even flat gather reaches 63% of the baseline and the topology-aware path reaches 90%; at 614436144^{3} the communication-to-compute ratio is higher, so flat gather collapses to 38% while the topology-aware path reaches 82%.

  • •

    Compute-core reuse. The topology-aware path uses the bf16 GEMM kernel (snake-swizzled 32×64×3232{\times}64{\times}32 DPAS, per-shape snake width) verbatim; no distributed-specific compute changes, so the single-GPU tuning carries over.

H.3. Methodology

All 12 GPUs run concurrently in a single process (12 SYCL queues, one per GPU), so the measurement includes intra-node fabric and shared power contention. Each method is timed as the median of 30 iterations after 10 warmup iterations and a 2 s turbo burn-in, identical to the single-GPU GEMM reference protocol. Every method is co-measured in the same run against the GEMM-only baseline, so all ratios are within-run. Inputs use Box-Muller N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) random initialisation (matching torch.randn) for the performance numbers; a separate constant-fill run gates correctness analytically (see the correctness discussion below). Per-GPU throughput is 2​M​N​K/t2MNK/t.

H.3.1. Controlled coding-agent task

Appendix C.5 reports the controlled coding-agent evaluation of the 614436144^{3} row-sharded operation, including its task definition, protocols, and correctness-gated results.

H.4. Engineer-Agent Co-Design

Our first engineering pass refined a kernel from the SyclKittens context. A subsequent common-harness comparison with Box–Muller N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) inputs measured the best SyclKittens and SyclKittens + examples kernels alongside that initial refinement. The SyclKittens + examples kernel reached 131.616 TFLOP/s, compared with 123.207 for the SyclKittens kernel and 128.545 for the initial refinement.

We restarted from the unchanged SyclKittens + examples kernel and retained it as the incumbent. The selected refinement preserves its DPAS compute core and staggered even/odd-plane cross-package gather. It changes only the MDFI replication phase, in which package bands are visited cyclically, with the first two copies assigned to the compute queue and the remaining four to the copy queue. Candidate promotion requires both a paired ratio above one and an absolute median-of-node-medians no lower than the incumbent.

Each repetition uses a 2-second burn-in, 10 warmups, and the median of 30 timed operations, with source order rotated across pairs. Both sources pass 4,096 sampled references on all 12 outputs before and after timing in all 56 executions; maximum post-timing relative L2 error is 8.67×10−78.67{\times}10^{-7}. The margin is small next to run-to-run variation. Across the 28 paired repetitions the median ratio is 1.007×1.007\times and the 95%95\% confidence interval on that ratio spans 0.93×0.93\times to 1.04×1.04\times, so the refined kernel is best read as matching the incumbent rather than beating it. We report it as the certified engineer-agent source because it wins the promotion protocol.

The study suggests enumerating collective placement over inputs, partial results, and outputs before tuning schedules, carrying topology routing across the chosen placement, and then retuning for the resulting local shard geometry. Our refinement protocol retains the strongest validated agent source as a selectable incumbent throughout tuning. An engineered variant is promoted only after it wins the same input, correctness, timing, and reduction protocol.

H.5. Topology-Aware All-Gather with Collaborative Prefetch

This path uses the same collaborative de-duplicated prefetch core as Appendix D. This cooperative-prefetch measurement is separate from the earlier fixed-core movement ablation’s 82% and 90% endpoints. Results are three-repetition medians on one quiet node; the distributed measurement includes the complete topology-aware all-gather and is normalized to the co-measured GEMM-only baseline.

The larger shape amortizes communication and reaches 93% of the local compute ceiling. The smaller shape is communication-bound but still retains 84%. Both shapes pass the analytic constant-fill correctness gate. The 113.1113.1-TFLOP/s result is not the campaign-local hand reference in Appendix C.5. That campaign uses its evaluator’s deterministic input distribution and a separately frozen build, while this table uses random-normal inputs and the cooperative-prefetch build. The coincident 134.9134.9 values in the two appendices are also different quantities. Here it is SyclKittens GEMM-only throughput with no communication; there it is the median end-to-end oneCCL all-gather plus oneDNN GEMM throughput.

Matched root-cause decomposition.

We rebuilt both configurations from the same frozen source and compiler, then co-measured them on four healthy nodes using three repetitions per condition, a 2-second burn-in, 10 warmups, and 30 timed operations. Table 50 reports the cross-node median of each node’s repetition median at 614436144^{3}.

H.6. Correctness

A separate constant-fill run (Alocal​[d]=(d+1)⋅0.01A_{\text{local}}[d]=(d+1)\cdot 0.01, B=0.01B=0.01) gives an analytic reference. The cooperative-prefetch GEMM-only and topology-aware distributed paths pass the max-diff <0.5<0.5 gate; the in-register bf16 RNE store is the only rounding source.

Appendix I Context-Parallel Attention (Ring and All-Gather)

Context-parallel attention combines the fence-free core from Appendix E with ring and all-gather KV distribution. Their memory footprints differ, so both paths are measured under the same performance and correctness gates on three clean nodes.

  • •

    Ring attention. Each active GPU holds one KV shard and rotates shards around the XeLink ring, so per-GPU memory is O(NperN_{\text{per}}). It supports contexts beyond one GPU’s HBM.

  • •

    All-gather attention. Each active GPU gathers the full NtotalN_{\text{total}} KV once (fan-out push all-gather) and runs a single flash pass, so per-GPU memory is O(NtotalN_{\text{total}}). When the gathered context fits in HBM, it pays the inter-package cost once instead of at each ring step.

Measurements use a clock-gated, three-node, ten-trial harness. The PyTorch paths pair ring (send/receive) and all-gather communication with both the autotuned 2-D-block-pointer Triton flash kernel used in Appendix E and an IPEX/aten fused flash kernel. Every functional variant passes the same correctness gate.

I.1. Configuration

Per-GPU TFLOPS uses 4​B​H​Nper​Ntotal​D4\,BH\,N_{\text{per}}N_{\text{total}}D because each GPU’s query shard attends the full context; this is directly comparable across methods and baselines.

I.2. Kernel Implementation and Key Techniques

Ring attention shards context across six GPU packages, with one active GPU stack each. At every step, each GPU computes partial attention for its local queries against the resident KV shard, rotates that shard one XeLink hop, and updates the online-softmax state. The ring implementation pairs independently tuned collective and compute implementations. Both methods use ThunderKittens tile primitives.

Data flow (per ring step, per active GPU).

Each step has three stages. First, the fence-free 256-work-item flash core with 16-query blocks from Appendix E computes partial OO/LSE for the local queries and resident KV shard. Second, the kernel merges the max, normalizer, and output accumulator into the running online-softmax state. Third, a double-buffered bulk memcpy moves the next KV shard from the ring neighbor through the shared SYCL context into the alternate local-HBM buffer. The in-order queue serializes compute and transfer, so the next step reads local HBM. The overlapped follow-up below uses copy engines to overlap rotation with compute.

Key techniques.
  • •

    Bulk-memcpy KV rotation. KV shards are copied in bulk to local HBM and attended locally. A measured zero-copy variant instead reads K/V over XeLink for each DPAS operation. Because these reads do not overlap asynchronously with the DPAS engine, that variant stalls compute and is 5–50×\times slower.

  • •

    Double-buffered rotation. Two KV buffers (current/next) keep the active and incoming shards separate. They also support the overlapped follow-up, which hides rotation latency behind compute at large NperN_{\text{per}}.

  • •

    Fence-free 256-work-item compute core. The same software-fence-free single-pass flash kernel used for single-GPU attention (Q preloaded once, IGC SWSB hazard ordering, split-D output, LPT launch order); about 15% faster at large NN than the earlier fence-heavy 128-work-item core it replaces.

  • •

    In-order queue serialization (no explicit fences between phases). The per-GPU in-order SYCL queue orders compute then rotate implicitly; no host-side event fence is inserted between the flash kernel and the rotation memcpy.

All-gather attention. Instead of rotating one shard per step, each active GPU gathers the entire NtotalN_{\text{total}} KV up front and runs one flash pass over the full context. Two techniques define this path.

  • •

    Fan-out push all-gather. Each active GPU reads its own KV shard once and writes it into the full [B,Ntotal,Hkv,D][B,N_{\text{total}},H_{\text{kv}},D] buffer of all five peers at its own slot in one parallel loop over cached peer pointers. The self-shard uses a local memcpy. This is the fan-out push pattern from the general-purpose all-gather in Appendix J. It sustains approximately 400 GB/s aggregate across the node, compared with the approximately 16 GB/s non-adjacent link that limits strict ring rotation and approximately 108 GB/s for the earlier fan-in pull gather.

  • •

    Single flash pass without online merge. The gathered KV is complete, so the validated 256-work-item core attends all NtotalN_{\text{total}} keys in one pass. The kernel already reads the KV buffer depth for the number of GPUs holding KV shards and uses NperN_{\text{per}} for the query grid, so Nq≠Nk​vN_{q}\neq N_{kv} needs only a thin dispatch wrapper, no softmax-merge reduction. Ring instead performs six rotations and online merges.

The trade-off is memory, because all-gather is O(NtotalN_{\text{total}}) per GPU and runs out of memory once the gathered context exceeds HBM, whereas ring stays O(NperN_{\text{per}}). Section I.4 quantifies the crossover.

I.3. Methodology

The ring uses the shared isolation protocol across six GPU packages, avoiding intra-package HBM contention. Each configuration runs 10 independent trials of 15 iterations. PyTorch ring trials reduce timing to the slowest rank with a max all-reduce. Results use the per-node median followed by the cross-node median and min–max spread over three nodes.

The PyTorch variants run on the same shards in the same harness. Ring baselines are sendrecv/aten, sendrecv/triton, and async/aten, the last using overlapped batched non-blocking send/receive. All-gather baselines are allgather/aten, the tuned vendor library path combining oneCCL all_gather with IPEX fused flash, and allgather/triton, which combines the oneCCL gather with autotuned Triton flash. These two are the algorithm-matched baselines for SyclKittens all-gather attention.

Every functional method is checked against a full-context attention reference before inclusion. The SyclKittens all-gather path is also verified in-binary against an online-softmax reference (§I.5).

I.4. Delivered Performance

Tables report cross-node median TFLOPS per active GPU over three clean nodes, with the node-level min–max spread in brackets; both methods use the same harness.

I.4.1. Ring attention

SyclKittens/PyTorch ratios compare SyclKittens ring attention with the blocking sendrecv ring baselines. The single-batch (B=1B=1) sweep covers 1.5K–98K total context (256–16384 tokens per GPU).

Against sendrecv/aten, the SyclKittens ring margin narrows from 1.85×\times at Nper=256N_{\text{per}}=256 to 1.05×\times at 16384; against sendrecv/triton, it remains 1.76–2.89×\times.

Table 52 reports the sequential schedule. Overlapping the shard rotation with compute on the copy engines raises the same six configurations to 1.7, 15.2, 31.7, 53.6, 60.7, and 69.0 TFLOP/s per GPU, which is 1.21–2.46×\times the aten ring and 1.45×\times at 49K total tokens (Figure 7(a)).

The step breakdown shows how rotation and online-softmax merge diminish relative to compute as the shard grows.

From Nper=256N_{\text{per}}=256 to 8192, the flash-core share rises from 20% to 65%, while reduction falls from 41% to 6% and rotation from 40% to 29%. Ring throughput therefore approaches the single-GPU attention efficiency in Appendix E as the shard grows.

I.4.2. All-gather attention

SyclKittens all-gather attention gathers the full context once and runs a single flash pass. Ratios are SyclKittens over each PyTorch all-gather baseline (same algorithm), plus SyclKittens all-gather over SyclKittens ring on the identical shard. Single-batch (B=1B=1) query shard swept 256–16384 per GPU (gathered context Ntotal=6×NperN_{\text{total}}=6\times N_{\text{per}}).

Relative to the sequential SyclKittens ring, the all-gather advantage narrows from 4.26×\times at Nper=256N_{\text{per}}=256 to 1.17×\times at 16384, while remaining 1.65–2.79×\times faster than allgather/triton. The tuned oneCCL-plus-IPEX path overtakes it only at the two largest shards, where the SyclKittens/aten ratios are 0.92×\times and 0.93×\times. At Nper=8192N_{\text{per}}=8192, the fan-out gather takes 4.7 ms (9%) and flash takes 46.3 ms (91%), so the flash pass controls throughput at this shape.

I.4.3. Memory-capacity trade-off

HBM capacity determines which path applies.

  • •

    Gathered context fits in HBM. All-gather pays the inter-package cost once and is 1.171.17–4.26×4.26\times faster than the sequential ring across the measured B=1B=1 sweep.

  • •

    Context exceeds one GPU’s HBM. Ring retains an O(NperN_{\text{per}}) footprint and increases supported context with the active GPU count.

The all-gather buffer holds six KV shards per GPU in this configuration. Ring stores only a constant number of shards, including its rotation buffers, so its KV memory per GPU scales with local rather than total context length.

I.5. Correctness

Every functional method is validated against an aten fused-flash full-context reference (relative error, bf16 in, fp32 accumulate). Representative maxima across the three nodes appear below.

All functional configurations pass (tolerance 0.05); the error falls with NperN_{\text{per}} as the softmax normalizer averages more terms. SyclKittens ring attention is validated by its own in-binary reference check on each shard, and SyclKittens all-gather attention is checked in-binary against an online-softmax full-context reference (relative error 0.0012 at Nper=256N_{\text{per}}=256, well under tolerance) before any timing is recorded.

Appendix J Multi-GPU Collectives

The SyclKittens collectives reduce per-call launch and handshake overhead. In a six-node matrix, all four win at the smallest standalone payload, 24 KiB, on every node. The evaluated batch-one decode uses two 8-KiB all-reduces per layer; this smaller payload is exercised in the end-to-end measurements in §K.5, not in the standalone sweep. Reduce-scatter also wins 0.19 MiB on every node, and destination-split all-to-all wins every measured payload on every node. Most other medium cells are node-sensitive. At 96 MiB, all-to-all is 1.20× faster on the median and wins all six nodes; oneCCL retains the median lead for all-reduce and all-gather, while reduce-scatter favors SyclKittens on four of six nodes. These paths also support distributed GEMM (Appendix H).

J.1. Configuration

We compare bf16 all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, and all-to-all on all 12 GPUs of one node containing six GPU packages. SyclKittens uses one process with shared-context peer pointers; the tuned vendor library path is oneCCL/xCCL with one process per GPU. Each SyclKittens collective dispatches adaptively between a latency-oriented path and a topology-aware bandwidth path.

J.2. Kernel Implementation and Key Techniques

Every SyclKittens collective builds on direct peer read/write, so GPU dd’s kernel addresses GPU kk’s HBM through the shared SYCL context, with a single host barrier per phase and no staging through host memory. Three measured techniques shape the per-collective kernels.

  • •

    Remote-write fan-out. On the measured peer route, a remote write sustains ∼\sim18.8 GB/s versus ∼\sim15.7 GB/s for a remote read. All-gather and large-payload all-reduce use fan-out push. Each GPU reads its local slice once and writes it to all N−1N{-}1 remote destinations. Local HBM reads cost e​p​depd rather than (N−1)​e​p​d(N{-}1)\,epd, leaving bandwidth for incoming remote writes and avoiding the HBM collapse of large-payload pull kernels.

  • •

    Hierarchical reduction. For all-reduce and reduce-scatter the hierarchical path first sums each GPU package’s two GPU stacks over MDFI, then reduces the partials from the six GPU packages over XeLink, halving the XeLink message count (the copy now carries already-summed data).

  • •

    Destination-split fused EU copy. For all-to-all, one kernel per source GPU pushes all NN chunks with by-value dispatch tables, while each workgroup owns one destination. This removes the per-message launch floor and exposes independent remote endpoints concurrently. The topology-aware all-gather uses the corresponding fused latency path.

The reduction and gather kernels dispatch adaptively between latency- and bandwidth-oriented paths. All-to-all uses the destination-split path at every size because it is neutral at the launch floor and wins as endpoint traffic grows.

J.2.1. Multi-GPU API

The collective kernels use the PGL peer-pointer table, Intel Max GPU topology planner, and system-scope atomic synchronization introduced in the tile-language appendix. These replace ThunderKittens’ CUDA NVLS multicast lowering while preserving explicit control over slice ownership, transfer direction, and schedule.

We validated the API conversion of all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce, and all-to-all against immutable pre-conversion binaries with complementary raw–API–API–raw and API–raw–raw–API orderings. Equal-weighting the two per-node bracket estimates gives an API/raw geomean of 1.013×1.013\times over all 28 operation–payload cells; the worst cell median is 0.974×0.974\times. Every cell passes the predefined 0.95×0.95\times guard and the aggregate passes the 0.99×0.99\times guard, establishing no material regression under the declared protocol.

A separate clean current-source recollection rebuilt all four production kernels and completed the full SyclKittens–oneCCL–SyclKittens matrix. All 336 SyclKittens rows passed full-buffer validation with zero mismatches, confirming the production build and oneCCL integration after conversion.

J.3. Methodology

Each same-node bracket runs SyclKittens and oneCCL on the same contiguous 12 GPUs and traverses the same physical MDFI and XeLink links under the same topology. The formal matrix repeats that bracket on six nodes. Each pass reports the median of 15 timed iterations after five warmups. For oneCCL, all_reduce(MAX) selects the slowest rank as the collective completion time.

All-reduce bandwidth uses 2​(N−1)/N⋅S/t2(N{-}1)/N\cdot S/t. All-gather, reduce-scatter, and all-to-all use the p2p-bytes convention N⁡(N−1)⋅e​p​d⋅2/tN(N{-}1)\cdot epd\cdot 2/t. The SyclKittens binary and its oneCCL counterpart print the same formula for aligned size sweeps, making their GB/s values directly comparable. Every node runs SyclKittens–oneCCL–SyclKittens; the SyclKittens value is the mean of its two bracketing medians, and speedup is paired on that node before taking the six-node median. Every SyclKittens point is full-buffer verified against a reference sum, gather, or scatter; maximum absolute error remains within bf16 rounding.

J.4. Delivered Performance

Tables report six-node marginal median μ\mus (12 GPUs), the matched-convention GB/s for both, and the median paired same-node speedup (oneCCL divided by SyclKittens; greater than 1 means SyclKittens is faster). Absolute performance tiers vary by node, so the paired speedup need not equal the ratio of the two marginal median times.

All-Reduce (busbw 2​(N−1)/N2(N{-}1)/N).

All-Gather (p2p bytes).

Reduce-Scatter (p2p bytes).

All-to-All (p2p bytes).

The crossover follows the dominant cost. At 24 KiB, all four SyclKittens collectives win all six nodes; reduce-scatter extends that robust win to 0.19 MiB and all-to-all extends it through 96 MiB. The medium AG/RS/AR ratios favor SyclKittens in the six-node median but cross parity between nodes. At 96 MiB, oneCCL wins AG, and AR in the median, RS favors SyclKittens on four of six nodes, and A2A favors SyclKittens on all six nodes. Thus the standalone sweep establishes the per-collective crossover from 24 KiB through 96 MiB; the smaller 8-KiB decode payload is evaluated in the complete decode path.

The decode orchestrator also replaces 64–96 per-token host waits with a system-scope atomic peer-counter barrier on the GPUs. This removes host serialization and improves multi-GPU decode TPOT by 1.1–1.54×, with the largest change on the 2D TP×\timesCP layout. The synchronization change does not alter arithmetic and passes the same correctness checks. It is used for the decode results in §K.5.

J.5. Correctness

Every SyclKittens collective is full-buffer verified on the participating GPUs against a reference on each run and each size, with all-reduce and reduce-scatter checked against an fp32 elementwise sum, all-gather and all-to-all against the exact gathered/permuted layout. Maximum absolute error is at most 0.01, within bf16 rounding. The oneCCL baseline uses the torch.distributed collective.

Appendix K End-to-End Llama-3.1-8B

On one GPU, composing SyclKittens operations with TorchInductor-generated regions improves Llama-3.1-8B full-request throughput by 1.59×1.59\times in geometric mean over torch.compile alone on the 21 configurations that both paths run. The composed path also serves the complete N=8192N=8192 grid, including cells where the baselines run out of memory. The final subsection evaluates multi-GPU decode separately.

K.1. Evaluated Kernel Set

Table 56 lists the implementations used for the measured end-to-end path. Each selection is the fastest correct implementation in its operation-specific study, and every run records the implementation that executes.

K.2. Baselines

Eager PyTorch executes the operator sequence directly. The torch.compile baseline fuses pointwise and reduction regions but graph-breaks at SDPA on this backend; all primary ratios compare the composed path with Inductor alone under identical compilation settings.

K.3. Operations across the SDPA Graph Break

SyclKittens supplies four operations across the attention graph break, namely GQA flash attention, joint Q/K rotary, a concatenated QKV projection, and residual-add plus RMSNorm. Inductor retains RMSNorm, SwiGLU, and the remaining pointwise and epilogue regions.

K.4. End-to-End Composition with TorchInductor

The integration boundary is the SDPA graph break. SyclKittens replaces regions that span this boundary, while TorchInductor continues to generate the remaining pointwise, reduction, and epilogue regions. Stand-alone norm and SiLU remain with Inductor because it matches or exceeds the corresponding stand-alone SyclKittens kernels.

Full-request metric.

Each repeat synchronizes the GPU, times one complete deterministic model.generate() call with max_new_tokens=128, and synchronizes again after return. For batch size BB, prompt length NN, mean actual generated sequence length G¯≤128\bar{G}\leq 128, and mean synchronized elapsed time t¯\bar{t} in seconds over the timed repeats, the harness records (B​N+G¯)/t¯(BN+\bar{G})/\bar{t}. This convention combines batch-wide prompt tokens with the mean generated length of one stream. We retain it for the reported full-request rates and ratios. Total batch-token throughput for equally long outputs would instead be B⁡(N+G¯)/t¯B(N+\bar{G})/\bar{t}. When compared runs generate the same lengths, the reported ratio equals their inverse elapsed-time ratio. The timed interval includes prefill and every generated decode step; compilation occurs during untimed warmup.

K.4.1. Configuration

Both composed and Inductor-alone runs use identical compilation settings, eight untimed warmups, and five synchronized repeats. The only difference is the four SyclKittens operations above; Inductor owns RMSNorm, SwiGLU, and all other pointwise and epilogue code generation in both runs.

K.4.2. Delivered performance

We evaluate bf16 Llama-3.1-8B on one GPU over 24 shapes with B∈{1,2,4,8}B\in\{1,2,4,8\} and N∈{256,512,1024,2048,4096,8192}N\in\{256,512,1024,2048,4096,8192\}. Composed, Inductor-alone, and eager runs are node-matched; the primary ratio is composed over Inductor alone. oom marks a baseline capacity failure.

For prefill at prompt length 256, the composed/Inductor ratio is 0.91×0.91\times–1.03×1.03\times. The projection GEMMs are too small to amortize the fused QKV, rotary, and residual launches, with 0.91×0.91\times at the 1×2561\times 256 cell. From prompt length 512 onward, the ratio increases with context, reaching 1.30×1.30\times at 8×20488\times 2048, 1.91×1.91\times at 4×40964\times 4096, and 2.03×2.03\times at 1×81921\times 8192 as the flash-attention path replaces the baseline attention path across the SDPA graph break.

Decode improves by 1.65×1.65\times geometrically and reaches 1.96×1.96\times at 1×2561\times 256. Decode is dispatch-bound; the SDPA graph break prevents Inductor from fusing the per-step attention prologue and epilogue, whereas the composed path uses fewer launches.

The harness retains only last-token logits, preventing a full-vocabulary all-position logits tensor from determining memory capacity. At N=8192N=8192, torch.compile runs out of memory at B​S≥2BS\geq 2 and eager at B​S≥4BS\geq 4. The composed path serves BS 1–8 at the prefill throughputs in Table 58 because its flash attention has the smaller memory footprint.

Across the N≤2048N\leq 2048 subset, the composed path retains a 1.56×1.56\times end-to-end geometric mean. The gain comes from combining Inductor’s pointwise/norm fusion with the cross-op and attention fusions that span its SDPA graph break; the flash-attention memory footprint also preserves coverage at long context.

K.5. Distributed Multi-GPU Decode (Single-Process TP+CP vs. oneCCL)

We measure Llama-3.1-8B decode on one node with six GPU packages, each with two stacks connected by MDFI. XeLink connects the GPU packages all-to-all through independent even and odd stack planes. A flat device hierarchy exposes all 12 stacks. We compare two implementations of tensor parallelism (Shoeybi et al., 2019). SyclKittens uses a single-process C++ orchestrator. The tuned Intel oneCCL library path uses torch.distributed with the xccl backend and one process per stack.

K.5.1. Configuration and compared implementations

The model has hidden size 4096, 32 query and 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, intermediate size 14336, and 32 layers. The node exposes six GPU packages and 12 stacks. Both systems use the same TP weight and KV sharding; SyclKittens uses inline peer collectives and can additionally shard KV by context.

K.5.2. Parallelization strategy

Decode combines a context-invariant weight stream with a KV scan that grows linearly with context. Tensor parallelism shards the weight stream, whereas context parallelism shards the growing KV term. The 2-D configurations below combine these schemes.

K.5.3. What SyclKittens runs per token

Each layer uses split-K flash decode for the KV scan, 128-bit wide-load GEMV for the five projections, inline peer all-reduce, and a GPU-side atomic rendezvous. The entire tile-by-layer loop is one C++ orchestrator call, so Python dispatch is removed from the inner loop. The C++ orchestrator still submits GPU work, and its cost is included in the measured decode time.

K.5.4. TPOT versus context

Table 61 reports steady-state time-per-output-token (TPOT), the geometric mean over 100 decode steps after prefilling to length NN; prefill is excluded. The p95 and p99 remain within 2 ms of the geometric mean throughout, and the medians coincide. Across matched two- and four-GPU configurations, SyclKittens is 1.521.52–2.91×2.91\times faster than the oneCCL-based decode path over the contexts where both run.

At 32K context SyclKittens on 2 GPUs is 2.89×2.89\times faster than oneCCL on 2 (36.2 vs. 104.6 ms) and on 4 GPUs 2.91×2.91\times (25.3 vs. 73.7 ms); equivalently SyclKittens sustains 39.5 tok/s on 4 GPUs at 32K versus oneCCL’s 13.6. At 128K the speedups are 2.43×2.43\times (P=2P=2) and 2.33×2.33\times (P=4P=4); at 256K, P=4P=4 is 1.52×1.52\times over xCCL w​s=4ws=4 and P=2P=2 runs at all where xCCL w​s=2ws=2 runs out of memory.

K.5.5. Per-layer collective cost

Each layer performs two all-reduces as inline single-process peer pulls over the shared context. A separate category-level profile assigns all-reduces about 1.7 ms/token at P=2P=2 and 3.1 ms/token at P=4P=4. In that instrumented profile, they account for 3.4–3.7% at short context and less than 1.5% after the KV scan dominates. The profiler synchronizes around categories, so these percentages describe its instrumented step breakdown, not the final overlapped TPOT table.

At fixed GPU count, this collective cost stays nearly constant as context grows, so its fraction of TPOT falls. The oneCCL path invokes a cross-process collective at each of the two reduction sites per layer; its two-GPU TPOT rises from 43 ms at 1K to 105 ms at 32K, while the SyclKittens path rises from 23 to 36 ms.

K.5.6. GPU count and capacity

Flat TP=4 has the lowest TPOT across the measured TP-only range. The 2-D measurements below evaluate longer contexts. The 128-KB/token KV cache exceeds one-GPU capacity at approximately 384K context, after which sharding is required for capacity.

K.5.7. 2D scaling to the full node (TP×CP\mathrm{TP}\times\mathrm{CP})

Plain TP is capped at P=8P=8 and loses efficiency before that limit. Context parallelism (CP) instead shards the KV cache by sequence position, computes a local flash partial on each GPU, and merges the softmax statistics across GPUs without a head-count limit. A standalone CP-attention prototype accelerates the 128K KV scan by 6.6×6.6\times across 4 GPUs and 8.5×8.5\times across 8, with maximum absolute error 10−410^{-4}.

The full 2-D orchestrator shards weights by TP and replicates them across CP, so CP leaves per-GPU GEMM work unchanged but replicates that work across CP groups. It shards the KV cache by sequence, merges the CP softmax partials within each TP group, and performs the two TP all-reduces per layer. One process drives all 12 GPUs.

The lowest-TPOT mapping is flat P=4P=4 through 32K, TP=2×CP=3\mathrm{TP}=2\times\mathrm{CP}=3 on six GPUs at 64K–128K, and TP=4×CP=3\mathrm{TP}=4\times\mathrm{CP}=3 on 12 GPUs at 256K. The six-GPU path measures 29.4, 31.0, and 45.4 ms at 32K, 64K, and 128K. At 64K and 128K it is respectively 1.76×1.76\times and 2.11×2.11\times faster than flat P=4P=4. The 12-GPU path remains at 59.0–60.0 ms through 128K, then reaches 73.3 ms at 256K, compared with 93.9 ms for six GPUs and 271.9 ms for flat P=4P=4. Both 2-D layouts use CP=3\mathrm{CP}=3; the additional TP sharding affects the largest KV scan.

With these additional GPUs, the measured ratio over the oneCCL-based decode path is 4.90×4.90\times at 128K (6-GPU 45.4 vs. w​s=4ws=4’s 222.3) and 5.63×5.63\times at 256K (12-GPU 73.3 vs. 413.0, where w​s=2ws=2 runs out of memory). These are scaling comparisons against four GPUs, not matched-resource speedups. Both selected layouts use the same single-process collective and GPU-side barrier.

K.5.8. Correctness methodology

The correctness gate uses first-new-token logit-vector cosine similarity against the single-GPU (P=1P=1) run. Greedy token matching varies across runs because fused SDPA reduction order changes near-tied argmax logits. In the broader validation sweep, which also includes eight GPUs, P∈{2,4,8}P\in\{2,4,8\} configurations reproduce P=1P=1 to cosine 0.99998 at dense context and 0.99973 at 128K–256K. The maximum absolute logit difference is 0.125, corresponding to bf16 rounding.
